subsubtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL-CANADIAN PACIFIC ACT JURISDICTION OF FEDERAL AUTHORITY OVER RATES OF PAY, HOURS OF WORK, ETC.
speechtext: The object of this bill is to amend the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act so as to give the federal authority jurisdiction over rates of pay, hours of work and certain working conditions of the employees of the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways. As the matter now stands the provinces, under property and civil rights, have passed their own legislation, and the result is that the collective agreements which have been entered into between the railways and their employees have not uniform application in all parts of the country. The purpose of this legislation is to occupy the field in so far as labour relations of railway workers are concerned.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CONDITIONS UNDER WHICH POLISH GIRLS ARE BEING BROUGHT TO CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, will the Minister of Labour now answer my question with respect to Polish girls?

subtopic: CONDITIONS UNDER WHICH POLISH GIRLS ARE BEING BROUGHT TO CANADA
speechtext:
In reply to a question asked last week by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) as to girls at present located in displaced persons camps in Europe being brought to Canada by the Dionne Spinning Mills of St. George, Beauce, Quebec, I would advise that the details of the arrangement are set out in order in council P.C. 1193.
With reference to the specific contracts which will be entered into by the girls with the Dionne Spinning Mills, they will provide for rates of wages no less favourable than those required by the provincial laws of Quebec.
My information is that it is the intention of the company to pay these girls the same rates of wages which prevail for other labour in the mill, and an order for return has been tabled which shows, according to reports to the Department of Labour, that no girls are employed at less than 25 cents an hour and that the average rate is 35 cents per hour. However, later information on the question of wages has been received in a telegram from Paul Baillargeon, attorney for the Dionne Spinning Mills, dated May 22, reading as follows:
Answering your telegram: Taken from one of our recent payrolls girl machine operators minimum for experienced beginner is twenty-five cents per hour paid for forty-eight hours weekly but only work forty-six. This equals approximately twenty-six cents per hour minimum. This is increased to thirty cents per hour after one month. After that they are paid according to what they produce. Our experienced girls earn up to a maximum of sixty cents per hour plus three per cent. They also receive two per cent of their weekly earnings for vacation pay. They receive group sick benefit and death insurance five hundred dollars for females. We have only two married women.
In further explanation I quote from Mr. Dionne's letter to my colleague, the hon. the Minister of Mines and Resources:
These girls will take their headquarters at the convent which is situated 500 feet from the mill and is under the direction of the Sisters of the Good Shepherd.
I will pay the transportation of these girls from their homes to Canada. I will see that
these girls or widows are healthy morally and physically. I will comply with the rules and regulations of the Canadian government.
I will make a contract with these girls to refund me their transportation charges at about 25 per cent of what they will earn weekly in my plant. I will pay these girls, when they begin to work, according to the ordinance No. 5 regulating the salaries and conditions of work of textile industries in the province of Quebec.
That is the end of the telegram.
In addition, the company has undertaken to return the girls to point of origin if the arrangement is not mutually satisfactory.
I now table copy of P.C. 1193 dated April 1, 1947, and other documents pertaining to this matter.
I thought my hon. friend1 would like to see the whole file.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, May 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie that the house go into committee on a resolution for the appointment of a joint committee of both houses of parliament to consider the question of human rights and fundamental freedoms.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in many respects I believe that this debate on a resolution to set up a special parliamentary committee to study human rights and fundamental freedoms is one of the most important debates that we shall take part in during the present session. It is one debate wherein we are not vying with each other in a discussion over the cost of this or that commodity or involving ourselves in a discussion of the pros and cons of some expenditure. To my mind it involves the discussion of the fundamental philosophy of our democratic way of life as against the philosophy of totalitarian slavery.
The terms of the resolution indicate that a good deal of thought has been put into it. I should like to read the resolution, and for the sake of brevity I will omit the names of the members of the joint committee. The resolution reads:
That a joint committee of both houses of parliament be appointed to consider the question of human rights and fundamental freedoms, and the manner in which those obligations accepted by all members of the united nations may best be implemented;
And, in particular, in the light of the provisions contained in the charter of the united nations, and the establishment by the economic and social council thereof of a commission on human rights, what is the legal and constitutional situation in Canada with respect to such rights, and what steps, if any, it would be advisable to take or to recommend for the purpose of preserving in Canada respect for and observance of human rights and fundamental freedoms;
It is a little difficult for me to detect all that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) may have had in mind when he worded that lesolution. I cannot conceive why in the whole matter of the united nations organization, with its charter and many complicated relationships, both economic and educational and commercial, and in matters of world justice and what have you, this one matter of human rights and fundamental freedoms should be singled out as being so important as to warrant the appointment of a special parliamentary committee to investigate, discuss and make recommendations.

Human Rights
As we are all aware, 1867 was the year of confederation, but Canada was a country and a nation long before that. It strikes me that Canadian citizens have always enjoyed what we regard as human rights and fundamental freedoms. Why is it necessary now, so many years after confederation, after so many years of life in a democracy, that we should begin to turn our attention to a delineation of these human rights and fundamental freedoms?
I have taken an intense interest in the speeches which have been made so far in this debate. Some of them have been filled with exceptionally good advice, but there have been some that I have not been able fully to understand. The other day I listened with a good deal of interest, as I usually do, to the able speech of the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart), but there were one or two things that I did not quite understand, indeed which appeared to me to be just a little self-contradictory. At page 3160 of Hansard I read, for instance, this paragraph:
Six hundred years ago they fought in Scotland against the foreign oppressor. They fought for the right of nationhood, and today there is still that same desire in the world for the right to self-determination.
I agree with that; I do most profoundly agree with the speaker on that point. But it does seem to me that that fundamental principle has already been done away with in some of our international gatherings. A few years ago we were all enamoured of a highly important and precious document known as the Atlantic charter. It had been signed by some of the big men of the earth. So far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, the Atlantic charter has become a scrap of paper, for in the negotiations carried on since the Atlantic charter was signed there has been little regard in many instances to giving the right of selfdetermination to some of the smaller nations.
The other day I read in the Toronto Star- I do read the Toronto Star occasionally-a British United Press dispatch from London, headed "Turks say U.S. aid is annoying Soviet," and the article reads:
The Turkish newspaper Aksam, which frequently reflects official opinion, said in an editorial broadcast by the Ankara radio today the U.S. aid programme has increased Russia's "hostile sentiments" toward Turkey.
The newspaper said Soviet policy would have to change if Soviet-Turkish relations were to improve.
"There is nothing we can do to renew the ties of friendship that we desire to have with Russia, for the conditions appear to be clear-cut," Aksam, said, outlining the conditions as:
"We have to give up the straits and Istanbul. We are to act an an enemy toward Great Britain and the United States. We are to set up a communist government, imported wholesale
from Russia. And nothing less than the whole thing will do, for if one single condition is turned down, Russia won't even look our way."
That is a very important press dispatch, for the reason that it does away completely with the right of small nations to their national self-determination. I do not know what the attitude of the hon. member for Winnipeg North would be towards the recent United States loan to Turkey, but I do know that the expressions in some circles from those holding socialist views are not very happy ones. Yet in this dispatch, which reflects very largely official opinion, I have read the attitude taken by Turkey.
Much has been said during recent months as to the necessity for the nations of the world giving up some of their national sovereignty. I must admit, Mr. Speaker, that I have never been able to fathom just what these advocates mean, because when rve ask them what part of our national sovereignty we are to give up, they never seem to know just what; they never seem to have an answer. While on this point I might mention our Canadian ambassador to Washington, who the other day in a speech bodly asserted that some of the nations would have to give up some of their national sovereignty. I might ask, Mr. Speaker, whether Mr. L. B. Pearson, our ambassador at Washington, was reflecting our official opinion in Canada, and if he was, who gave him authority to make that statement that we had to give up some of our national sovereignty? The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) is in his seat, and he can answer that if he wishes. I do say this, that diplomats as a rule are very careful about breaking into print, and I should like to know who gave the right to Mr. Pearson to make that statement, and whether it does reflect official opinion in this country. Furthermore, if it does reflect official opinion, I say that this parliament has a right to know from the present administration what part of our national sovereignty we must surrender. So far, while in past years this phraseology has been shouted from the housetops, we have not yet heard what part of our national sovereignty we must surrender.
The other day at a dinner given by the health league I heard one of Canada's eminent scientists speak on the atom bomb. His message was most interesting and deserved a good deal of commendation. I wish that that message might be put into print and circulated throughout Canada. But this was the part to which I took exception. Somehow or other before he finished-and I said to myself as he was coming to this point, "Ah, here it is; I thought so!"-he said that we should have to surrender some of our national
Human Rights

sovereignty. I do not know why he had to conclude on that note. I often think of the little phrase in scripture when our Lord was before Pilate and Pilate said something to him. Our Lord turned to him and said: "Sayest thou this thing of thyself, or did others tell it thee?" I just wonder how many of these men in important positions speak the words of truth and soberness as their own original thoughts, or whether somebody whispers something in their ear and as a result they are reflecting what they may think is a popular phrase, something that is in the air.
Here we are in this parliament-

What I was talking about was the selling out or the surrendering of a part of our national sovereignty. Let the government state what it is we are surrendering. I am fearful that when these men in high places talk that way what they mean is that we are to surrender something of our human rights and fundamental freedoms.
I go further in my analysis of the speech of the hon. member for Winnipeg North. He talks about racial discrimination. I am not going to labour the point, but at page 3161 of Hansard he says:
. . . where racial discrimination and intolerance of another's religious beliefs will be regarded as crimes against all mankind; where freedom of speech will be the inalienable right of every citizen.
That paragraph is self-contradictory, because if I am to be charged under the criminal code or if it is to be regarded as a criminal offence for me to criticize another religion, then I have not free speech. I say that I have the right to criticize another man's religion, and he has the same right to criticize mine. It is all very well to confine this to religion, but take political beliefs-I am not talking about party machine politics now, but we have come to the place in the world's history when there are political beliefs on a world-wide scale which are, I was going to say, almost tantamount to being a religion.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: They are.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE

They are to a very large extent. In the debate on the speech from the throne the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) referred to socialism as being a new way of life that was dawning upon society, or words to that effect. I take issue with him as to its being a new way of life; it is about as old as mankind itself. But that is neither here nor there. A way of life is certainly as potent as a religion. If it is to be thought a criminal act to criticize a philosophy of life, then I have not freedom of speech. You cannot have it both ways.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North, referring to Jehovah's Witnesses, said as reported at page 3162 of Hansard:
We w'ill deplore perhaps the way they say it; and yet I maintain as a democratic citizen that they are entitled to freedom to sav it so long as they do not violate the laws of the land. =
I agree with that, but how can you reconcile that with the former statement that it should be regarded as a criminal act to criticize another religion or sect? I should like that explained. I often w'onder what some people mean by racial discrimination. I have the greatest respect for all other races of man. The good Lord created everyone, but I wonder whether it is to be regarded as racial discrimination if a man in a restaurant displays a sign, "All white help". If fundamental freedom means anything it means that if a man wishes to display a sign of that kind he should be able to do so. Why not? He is in business. If he does not get business it is his own fault.
I wonder whether it would be right for a man to have a Japanese valet. Perhaps because the Japanese will not associate with his friends he would like to have a Japanese valet. What would happen if a Canadian or an English butler applied for the job? Is the employer to be considered subject to the criminal code if he says, "No, I am sorry, I cannot employ you; I want a Jap". If a man wants to employ a Jap I think he should have the right to do so. That is one of the fundamental freedoms we have.
I do not claim to know everything about socialism-

That is the big idea in socialism. Let us remember this. God created every one of us, black or white, yellow, red, it does not matter what the colour of the skin may be; He created every individual with a soul. But the same God who created us said that He had fixed the bounds of men's habitation. We can tear those bounds down,
I suppose, because sometimes we dare to assume we are a little wiser than the omniscient.

I do not distinguish
between world socialism and world communism. Somebody said the other day that the C.C.F. were Liberals in a hurry. I would say the communists are socialists in a hurry. That is all there is to it as far as I am concerned. The member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) in this debate referred to the socialization of land. Our C.C.F. friends deny that. I do not say they are going to do that in Saskatchewan;
I am not so bold as to say that. As a matter of fact, I know the premier of Saskatchewan quite well. We sat in the house together. He is a fine gentleman. I do not think he would want to socialize the land, but I would say that fundamentally socialism dares to propose the socialization of land. I am dealing with the philosophy of socialism. I had a book put into my hands some time ago by a friend of mine. The title was "The Case for Socialism". The author is Fred Henderson. I may say my friend bought this book at one of the C.C.F. meetings. I have copied certain extracts in my own hand, and at page 22 I find the following:
It is this private ownership of land and capital which we socialists indict as the root cause of poverty. We challenge its justice and its right to exist or continue. We trace directly to it the ruin, the widespread misery and the destitution, of the mass of the people.
Then at page 24:
As for land ownership-well, it is hardly necessary nowadays to be a socialist to see that most Liberals and many orthodox politicians admit, that there is, and that there can be, no moral or just title whatever to the private ownership of land.
I can read more.

At page 31 of the same book I read:
Let there be no mistake about it. Socialism, I repeat, is an attack upon the institution of private property in land and capital. We socialists advocate the expropriation of the landed and capitalist class;
And on page 32:
I want you to be perfectly clear about this and not to attempt to shirk the full consequence of the socialist proposal. Do not, for example, let us deceive ourselves into thinking that we can get around this accusation about confiscation and robbery by talking about some form of compensation to the persons whom we propose

to expropriate. If the nation gave them compensation, in the sense of giving them the equivalent of what it is proposed to take from them, we should fail in our purpose.
Fundamentally, I began to learn some of these things as I read some of the books which were advocated by socialist-minded people.

I am not going to detain the house. All I wish to say is this. I do not know whether all members of this committee have the same conception of what human rights and fundamental freedoms are, but I say that the world is built upon law and order. The universe is built upon law and order, and it behooves all people to be subject to law, order and good government. There is a liberty which does not recognize authority, and that sort of liberty becomes licence. I have a strong feeling that the conception of human rights and fundamental freedoms of some members of the committee is going to be almost diametrically opposed to the conception of human rights and fundamental freedoms of other men on that committee.
Our socialists-let me interject this here- every once in a while take a crack at private enterprise. I am going to say that private enterprise is nothing more or less than the exercise by individuals of their human rights and fundamental freedoms.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE

When I say that, I do not modify my statement. I only point out that there are abuses in private enterprise, but it is not private enterprise that is at fault but the abuses, and we have to correct those abuses. My hon. friends laugh a little, giggle a little, but that does not concern me. I say that if "fundamental freedoms and human rights" means anything it means that a man has the right to do business with anyone who will do business with him. If that is private enterprise, all right.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I see that your eye is on the clock as well as on me, so I take it my time is pretty well gone. I close with a quotation from Major C. H. Douglas, whom some of us claim to be one of the greatest minds in the world today. He says:
In our anxiety to make a world safe for democracy it is a matter of real urgency that we do not tip out the baby with the bath water, and, by discarding too soon what is clearly an agency which can be made to operate both ways, make democracy even more unsafe for the individual than it is at present.

I close on that note. I say what we have to do in this committee is guard the human rights and fundamental freedoms that Canada has enjoyed ever since confederation. Nothing has changed in Canada, except that we have had the infiltration of a type of philosophy that would prepare our minds and soften us up for the acceptance of something that is diabolically evil.

subtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DISALLOWANCE AND RESERVATION OF BILLS

speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs) moved the second reading of Bill No. 20, to amend the Publication of Statutes Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill is fully explained in the explanatory note published with the bill itself. Under the act which determines the distribution to be made of the Canadian statutes it was provided that copies would be supplied to the governor general to be transmitted to one of the principal secretaries of state of His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom for consideration by the government of the United Kingdom, to the end that they be disallowed or allowed to operate, and also that certain bills might be reserved by the governor general for His Majesty's pleasure. In the conference of 1926, when the Balfour declaration was made, the question arose as to what would be the position with respect to the possible disallowance of dominion legislation by His Majesty on the advice of his ministers of the United Kingdom, and what was the position that had been reached with respect to reserving bills for the consideration of His Majesty on the advice of his United Kingdom ministers.

Publication oj Statutes Act
The question was left to be dealt with by the conference of jurists which was set up to determine what were the practical steps to be adopted to carry out the principle embodied in the Balfour declaration. That commission met in 1929, and with respect to disallowance unanimously made this recommendation, which is to be found at page 16 of the report of the conference on the operation of dominion legislation and merchant shipping legislation, 1929:
The conference agree that the present constitutional position is that the power of disallowance can no longer be exercised in relation to dominion legislation. Accordingly, those dominions who possess the power to amend their constitutions in this respect can, by following the prescribed procedure, abolish the legal power of disallowance if they so desire. In the case of those dominions who do not possess this power, it would be in accordance with constitutional practice that, if so requested by the dominion^ concerned, the government of the United Kingdom should ask parliament to pass the necessary legislation.
In respect of reservation the recommendation, which is to be found at page 19 of the report, is as follows:
Applying the principles laid down in the imperial conference report of 1926, it is established first that the power of discretionary reservation if exercised at all can only be exercised in accordance with the constitutional practice in the dominion governing the exercise of the powers of the governor general; secondly, that His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom will not advise His Majesty the King to give the governor general any instructions to reserve bills presented to him for assent, and thirdly, as regards the signification of the king's pleasure concerning a reserved bill, that it would not be in accordance with constitutional practice for advice to be tendered to His Majesty by His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom against the view of the government of the dominion concerned.
That being the constitutional practice, on April 5,	1943, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made a declaration in the House of Commons in answer to a question submitted by the hon. member for Temis-couata (Mr. Pouliot) to this effect:
It has never been the practice for the clerk of the parliaments to send bound copies of the Statutes of Canada to the British Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs. On certain occasions, namely during the years 1927 to 1942 inclusive, they have been sent by the Secretary of State for External Affairs who, since the arrangement concluded at the imperial conference in 1926, has been the recognized channel of communication between the government of Canada and the government of the United Kingdom.
The purpose of transmitting the Statutes of Canada in this manner has been to comply with the provisions of the Publication of Statutes Act and of section 56 of the British North America Act.
In 1942, in view of the complete obsolescence of the power of disallowance, and in order to bring the actual practice into conformity with the constitutional position the transmission from the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs was stopped.
That has been the situation in fact since that time. But there is still in the Publication of Statutes Act a provision which requires the Clerk of Parliaments to send bound copies to the Secretary of State for External Affairs for transmittance. Since 1942, instead of being transmitted to the United Kingdom, they have been sent to the library of the houses of parliament here. Nevertheless-

subtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DISALLOWANCE AND RESERVATION OF BILLS
speechtext:
These houses of parliament?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: To our Canadian houses of parliament. Nevertheless, though it was suggested that the Department of External Affairs tell the Clerk of Parliaments that he no longer need send them, it was felt that that would not be proper. There is a statute which places that duty upon the Clerk of Parliaments. And until parliament relieves him of that duty, it was felt that no one could give him instructions to disregard it. So the purpose of this bill is to amend the statutes respecting the publication of statutes, and thus relieve the Clerk of Parliaments of the obligation placed upon him by parliament, which is now without any practical object.

subtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DISALLOWANCE AND RESERVATION OF BILLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill No. 20, letter E of the senate, is one which has caused me considerable concern, and one about which the house should have some clarification as soon as possible. The debates in another place, to which I am not permitted to refer in detail, consisted largely in an explanation of the bill itself by its sponsor. Little or no debate took place there, and for that reason we have no explanations before us by those in the senior chamber with respect to points which might normally be raised in the house. What was said in introduction by the hon. senator in the other place w7as much the same as has been said today by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent).
Looking through the bill and the various statutes connected with it I find there are a number of matters concerning which I should like to have some explanation when the bill reaches committee of the whole. First of all it should be made clear that the Publication of Statutes Act, which is chapter 2 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, is one which deals with the subject matter indicated by its title. Today we are not interested in the

Publication of Statutes Act

repeal of the whole statute which was passed in 1925 by the parliament of Canada, but we are directing our attention to those parts of the statute which have to do with the publication of our statutes in the United Kingdom. If I may say so, it seems to me we cannot separate that part of the Publication of Statutes Act from the British North America Act itself.
Let me bring to the attention of the house the two sections of the British North America Act which is seems to me bear directly on this bill. Chapter 56 of the British North America Act states:
Where the governor general assents to a bill in the queen's name, he shall by the first convenient opportunity send an authentic copy of the act to one of Her Majesty's principal secretaries of state, and if the queen in council within two years after receipt thereof by the Secretary of State thinks fit to disallow the act, such disallowance (with a certificate of the secretary of the day on which the act was received by him) being signified by the governor general, by speech or message to each of the houses of parliament or by proclamation, shall annul the act from and after the day of such signification.
And section 56 states:
A bill reserved for the signification of the queen's pleasure shall not have any force unless and until within two years from the day on which it was presented to the governor general for the queen's assent, the governor general signifies, by speech or message to each of the houses of parliament or by proclamation, that it has received the assent of the queen in council.
An entry of every such speech, message or proclamation shall be made in the journal of each house, and a duplicate thereof duly attested shall be delivered to the proper officer to be kept among the records of Canada.
I read those two sections to show that the British North America Act was clear as to the power of disallowance; and I shall proceed from that point. It was because of section 56 of the British North America Act that section 6 of the Publication of Statutes Act, now to be repealed, was passed. That section states:
As soon as practicable after the prorogation of every session of parliament, the Clerk of the Parliaments shall obtain from the king's printer a sufficient number of bound copies of the Statutes of Canada passed during such session of parliament, and shall deliver to the governor general one copy duly certified, for transmission to one of His Majesty's principal secretaries of state, as required by the British North America Act 1867.
And- then it goes on to indicate that certified copies of all bills, along with certain other things, shall be delivered. The two acts, the British North America Act and the Publication of Statutes Act, especially section 6, are linked together; the one is woven into the fabric of the other.

The minister has indicated that on April 5, 1943, certain questions were asked with respect to this by the hon. member for Temiscouata. I do not think that I need to read the questions and answers in full, but I should like to indicate their general purport and significance.
It would appear that in 1942 the government stopped sending any further bound copies of the Statutes of Canada to the dominions office in London. As t'he minister pointed out, prior to that and after the Balfour declaration the procedure had been altered somewhat whereby the Secretary of State for External Affairs sent bound copies rather than the Clerk of the Parliaments. I have found out in my explorations that the Clerk of the Parliaments is actually the Clerk of the Senate. The channels through which the copies of the statutes were sent were changed from the Clerk of the Parliaments to one of His Majesty's principal secretaries, and they then went from the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the dominions office in London.
That went on from around 1930 until 1942. According to the answer given to the hon. member for Temiscouata, to be found on page 1828 of Hansard of April 5, 1943, the practice was then discontinued. The reason given by the Prime Minister was this, and I quote from page 1829:
The purpose of transmitting the Statutes of Canada in this manner has been to comply with the provisons of the Publication of Statutes Act and of section 56 of the British North America Act.
I have already put parts of those statutes on the record. The Prime Minister then goes on to say:
In 1942, in view of the complete obsolescence of the power of disallowance, and in order to bring the actual practice into conformity with the constitutional position, the transmission from the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs was stopped.
So far as I can gather there was no change from 1931 until 1942 with respect to our constitutional position, and in 1942 the government sent for the last time the Statutes of Canada to the United Kingdom. It may have been that the matter was overlooked in the meantime, but I think we are entitled to some explanation from the minister as to why they were stopped in that particular year. I am wondering -if they were stopped because the hon. member for Temiscouata put the questions he did on the order paper at that time It. would seem that up until the time the questions were put on the order paper and the answers given, the statutes had been going regularly through that last mentioned channel and without any hindrance or stoppage by the present government.

Publication oj Statutes Act
There is one point upon which I am not at all clear. A few moments ago the minister for external affairs referred to the conference of jurists which was held in 1929 for the purpose of giving an opinion as to our position, having in mind the Balfour declaration and the .changes brought about by the two imperial conferences held in the late twenties, the conference in 1930 being the last one held in respect to that. One thing which the minister tried to explain to the house was in reference to page 16 of the report of the conference of jurists, or commission of jurists, as he was pleased to call it. They agreed that any self-governing dominion could abolish the legal power of disallowance if they so desired, and it is upon those words that I want to build another point in my argument.
The British North America Act by section 56 plainly gives the power of disallowance. The conference of jurists indicated that that power could be abolished by the parliament of a self-governing dominion. The Statute of Westminster, passed in 1931, does not amend the British North America Act, and consequently does not amend section 56, which provides for the power of disallowance in the other parliament. While I understand clearly what the minister says with respect to the effect of the Statute of Westminster and its wide significance so far as our nationhood is concerned, still that statute provides by section 7:
Nothing in this act shall be deemed to apply to the repeal, amendment or alteration of the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1930, or any order, rule or regulation made thereunder.
Having made a careful check of the amendments to the British North America Act since 1930 I find that there has been none which could in any way be stretched to include section 56 which calls for the power of disallowance by the United Kingdom. That being so, I only want to go into the matter as fully as possible in order to see if we cannot clarify our position. According to the statutes which I have brought to the attention of the house this afternoon, that power of disallowance is still outstanding. It seems to me that this legislation either goes too far or it does not go far enough. Tied in as it is with section 56 of the British North America Act this bill is neither flesh nor fowl nor good red herring. should like to know from the minister when we are in committee what obsolescence means.

The other point I would raise is this. When the terms of the Statute of Westminster were agreed upon by the various members of the commonwealth, were changes such as this discussed and decided upon? Why is this matter arising now, some seventeen years afterwards? Also I would ask what about the other members of the British commonwealth of nations? What is their procedure in matters such as this, having in mind the Statute of Westminster itself. The house is entitled to know these things. On the surface this bill appears to be an innocuous piece of legislation. When I first looked at it, it seemed as though we might as well put in statutory form what we have been doing and that is drop the practice of sending these statutes across to the old country. But there is much more to it than appears on the surface, because, as I have tried to show, it goes to the root of an important principle with respect to the British commonwealth of nations.
This brings me to another point which I would like to impress upon the government. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, it is time that the members of the British commonwealth of nations ought to be less shy about each other and that they should try to arrange for more regular, frank, man-to-man talks among themselves. They expect that we shall get together as units of the commonwealth and clarify our position, and that our constitutional position shall be brought up to date where that needs to be done. Canada stands in a splendid position in regard to the commonwealth. It would not surprise me, even if it should other members of the house, if in the years that lie ahead this country became the centre of a greater and more powerful British commonwealth of nations. More than that, I am one of those who have always revelled in the fact that Canada is an autonomous nation in that great, happy and peaceful family of nations. But at the same time I think that Canada's most brilliant prospects as a nation will be heightened and brightened by taking a more active lead in this great peace-loving family of nations of which we are so proud to form a part.

Is it the minister's opinion that this particular part of the Publication of Statutes Act is in any different position from that of section 56 of the British North America Act?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Section 56 of the British North America Act now provides for something which a general conference of the governments of the autonomous units of the commomvealth have declared formally to be obsolete. It has become a recognized practice that disallowance will not be recommended by ministers of His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom with respect to any legislation of an autonomous dominion. That is the constitutional status which has been attained. It has also been declared that the parliament of the United Kingdom would not undertake to legislate for an autonomous dominion unless it be at the request of that dominion. That is the present constitutional situation. If, in spite of that, the parliament of the United Kingdom chose to reenact the Colonial Laws Validity Act and to attempt again to treat the units of the commonwealth as subordinate colonies, in theory it might still be the legal effect of such statutes, but it would not work. It would not operate; it would be the death-knell of the commonwealth association.
We could have proceeded to submit joint addresses to ask that the terms of section 56 of the British North America Act be modified, but whenever we do attempt any modification whatsoever of the British North America Act we have a pretty active controversy in this country. Today it is not desirable to have these controversies unless we are going to achieve something as a result of the controversy. When it is merely something that is academic the controversy is undesirable.
In 1940 the hon. member for Temiscouata brought up this matter of transmitting our statutes and he was told what- the practice then was. The hon. member just slightly qualified what I had said. Before 1926 the channel of communication between a dominion and His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom was the Governor General. That was the original position. He was the representative of the government of the United Kingdom; he was the channel through which the dominion communicated. Then the usual process by which constitutional changes have come about wdthout revolution in British countries operated and the Governor
General got into the position where, in fact, his constitutional relationship with his ministers in Canada was the same as the constitutional relationship of His Majesty with his ministers in the United Kingdom. That became the situation in fact, recognized as such, and the channel of communication between the Canadian government and the government of the United Kingdom became the office of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I do not mean to assert that we are to have an embargo on the export of statutes to the United Kingdom. As a matter of fact they still go. They need them for their own information as we need theirs for our information.
But here is a provision in a Canadian statute which states that certain copies are to be sent for a certain purpose, and that purpose has entirely disappeared. Therefore the proposal that was made originally came up in 1940 and in 1942. It was proposed that the Clerk of the Parliaments be told not to comply with the Publication of Statutes Act. That proposal was not accepted. It was felt that it would not be proper for the government to attempt to say that a servant of parliament would not do what parliament had said he should do, and that if he was not to do it parliament should be asked to make the necessary statement. That is what the bill is for. It would be quite as logical to have addresses to modify section 56 of the British North America Act; but my hon. friend knows what suspicion would be aroused. Any attempt at this time to get an amendment to the constitution would give rise to serious controversy. There would be some who would say that it is not going far enough. I was horrified to read in one of the papers of my province that the new editor appointed to direct the course of that paper was advocating a Canadian republic. To have any controversy over whether we are to have at this time a Canadian republic or not would be. I think, a pretty futile one, one that would not lead to any practical result and would stir up a lot of feeling for nothing. Why not deal only with the things that will achieve some practical result and not unnecessarily stir up controversy that does engender some bitterness and produce no good. Therefore it was felt that the only unnecessary thing that was still being done was that the Clerk of the Parliaments was complying with this requirement of a Canadian statute.

subtopic: POWERS OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL WITH RESPECT TO ARTICLE 41

speechtext: Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs) moved the second reading of Bill No. 132, respecting article 41 of the charter of the united nations.

subtopic: POWERS OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL WITH RESPECT TO ARTICLE 41
speechtext:
I expect the minister will want to make some explanation, and I myself have some remarks to offer.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Under the charter of the united nations, approved by both houses of the Canadian parliament, it is provided that

there shall be, as the principal organ for the maintenance of security among the united nations, a security council. The charter provides three phases of procedure in dealing with disputes which may arise between nations. The first is the phase of conciliation, when the security council uses its best endeavours to get the parties to the dispute to agree to remove the cause of the dispute. If the procedure of conciliation fails, then article 41 of the charter empowers the security council to decide upon non-military sanctions, which will be applied to a recalcitrant state. The council may decide what measures, not involving the use of armed force, are to be employed to give effect to its decisions; and it may call upon members of the united nations to apply such measures. These may include complete or partial interruption of economic relations and of rail, sea, air, postal, telegraphic, radio, and other means of communication, and the severance of diplomatic relations.
That is the article which gives to the security council the power to make these decisions. Under article 25, to which we have agreed:
The members of the united nations agree to accept and carry out the decisions of the security council in accordance with the present charter.
As hon. members know, the Canadian government can enter into international arrangements. But the action of the Canadian parliament is required to make it obligatory for Canadian citizens to do the things that may be necessary to carry out t'he international obligations assumed by the Canadian government.
At the present time there does not seem to be any urgent need for action to implement decisions under article 41 of the charter. Unfortunately-at least I regard it as unfortunate-proceedings in the security council have dragged to an extent and to a degree that has appeared to be disappointing and not to give us the feeling that it was capable and willing to take an active hand in preventing international strife. Nevertheless we have agreed to the charter. It is the only international instrument we have at the present time, and members on all sides of the house have declared that they support the policy of doing everything Canada can do to make the united nations succeed.
That being the attitude, we do not want to be subject to any reproach that any act or omission of ours was a reason for delay in having the united nations and the security council fully operative. We therefore ask parliament to authorize the governor in council. should occasion arise, to make such orders binding upon Canadian citizens as might be required to carry out Canada's obligations

United Nations
under articles 41 and 25 of the charter of the united nations in respect of non-military sanctions imposed by the security council upon a recalcitrant member of the united nations organization.
Similar legislation has been passed by the parliament of the United Kingdom and by the parliament of New Zealand. It has not yet been passed by the parliament of Australia, or that of South Africa. Similar legislation is not required in the United States. When the united nations charter was approved by the American Senate, that made it the law of the land; and it is in all respects a part of the law of the United States. So that the executive government there has power to carry it out. It is there in such form as to bind the individual American citizen.
Here, under our system, international treaties do not have a binding effect upon individuals because it is not normally within the power of the government to impose obligations upon citizens. It is only by parliament that that can be done; and this bill is recommended to parliament to empower the governor in council to take by order in council such action as we might be required to take by a directive of the security council.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the procedure in Canada in respect of this legislation has been somewhat similar to that taken by the parliament of the United Kingdom. This is another piece of legislation which has come from the other chamber for our attention. The same procedure was followed in the United Kingdom. Over there the debates showed clearly, as they took place on April 5, 1946, in the House of Commons at Westminster, that there was a unanimity of opinion which, in view of the present situation in the British House of Commons, is a matter of interest.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) referred to two sections of the charter of the united nations which deal with and bear upon the legislation now before us. Article 25 says:
The members of the united nations agree to accept and carry out the decisions of the security council in accordance with the present charter.
And article 41 says:
The security council may decide what measures not involving the use of armed force are to be employed to give effect to its decisions, and it may call upon the members of the united nations to apply such measures. These may include complete or partial interruption of economic relations and of rail, sea, air, postal, telegraphic, radio, and other means of communication, and the severance of diplomatic relations.
The United Kingdom was the first nation with a constitution requiring such legislative 83166-220
action to pass this provision. During t^e debates in the House of Commons at Westminster, reference was made from time to time to the fact that they were pioneering.
In my view the legislation before us does not necessarily involve a question of principle, because we must remember that we are bound by the principle of the charter. It does, however, deal at length with the method to be employed, and which we intend to employ in carrying out the undertakings we have already given when we attached our signatures to the San Francisco charter. In the bill before us wide and sweeping powers are given the executive. Perhaps I need not place on record the language of the bill itself, because it is in the hands of hon. members. I understand that when the bill went to the other place it was even more sweeping in its characteristics than it is now. After considering it in their house and in a committee, the honourable members of the other place succeeded in changing, altering and restricting the penalties. But even now the bill is not quite as sweeping as the one passed by the United Kingdom parliament. There are some suggestions which I have to make, based upon those which received the sanction of that parliament and which. I think, could be properly applied and would, I believe, strengthen and better the legislation now before this chamber.
The restrictions in connection with penalties are not to be found in a corresponding way in the United Kingdom legislation. Under normal circumstances I think this house would rebel against the giving of such wide and sweeping powers to the executive at the present time. However, there are perhaps arguments which the government will want to use to the effect that this situation is different from the one we would normally face in the domestic field. May I say that whatever happens to this legislation, whatever sweeping powers are given under this legislation, it must not be considered as a precedent in the domestic field.

This is a move in time of peace rather than in time of war, and the question was raised as to whether or not certain items in the legislation are beyond the purview of the dominion pailiament to enact. with raising that question. If we are to have the power in Canada, it must be constitutional power. I raise this question in order that the minister may reply later. One member in the other place referred to this bill as having teeth in it. I have not been able to find anything but false teeth in most of the enactments that have been passed by the united nations up to date. In all fairness and frankness, one has to admit that up to the present time there has not been much in the way of teeth in the heavily endowed organs of the new world organization.
While this bill went to a committee in the other place, we have had no full report from that committee. I should like to ask the minister under what act such as this Canada had the right to apply sanctions under the old league of nations. I should like to know whether any such bill was passed and, if so, when? Our part in the sanctions of 1935 was not something that many Canadians can look back upon with any great degree of glowing pride. I think we all remember when statesmen in Canada, I suppose supported by public opinion, suggested that the Abyssinian dispute was not worth the life of a single Canadian soldier. Perhaps that was so; but whatever happened, whether it was the accumulation and combination of the Abyssinian and other disputes, finally we reached the position where we lost not just one single Canadian soldier but 39,500 in all branches of the services only a few years afterward. That gives one some idea of how we should look back upon these sanctions.
We had our experience before with economic sanctions and I took the trouble to look up the newspaper reports of 1935. When one could find news of the sanction problem among the returns from the general elections of that particular period he found something like the following, which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of November 4, 1935:
The league of nations subcommittee on economic sanctions approved in principle today

the Canadian proposal that petroleum, coal, iron and steel be added to the prohibited list-introduced Saturday by Doctor W. A. Riddell to committee of 18.
Then the Ottawa Journal of November 16, 1935, contained this:
Canada moves in sanctions against Italy. Necessary order in council reported passed by government.
Then on December 2, 1935, the same paper stated that Mr. Riddell was silent on the stand that the government had taken, that only his personal opinions were represented and not the views of the Canadian government when he took the step he did in connection with oil sanctions against Italy. The Standard of London said:
Canada makes news. Her government has repudiated responsibility for the proposed oil sanctions against Italy. Today's declaration indicates a big break in the ranks of the sanction-ist nations.
We have travelled a long way since then. When we are speaking about the glowing future, it is always worth while to stop and take an inventory of the not too glorious past. That is why I have brought up the questions I have today. We have gone a long way since the day when a statesman representing Canada at the league of nations-it is really not so long ago-said that Canada was in a favoured position in that she lived in a fireproof house so far as world affairs were concerned. We have gone a long way since then, and it is a good job that we have. We have now reached the point where the house is being asked to give a body outside Canada, a body upon which there may not necessarily be Canadian representation, the right to sever our trade, our communications and our diplomatic relationships. The government is now asking parliament to give it the power to carry that out. It is not proper to raise grave questions about that at this moment, and I am not doing so. I am only indicating the distance to which parliament and the people of Canada appear to have gone. We are now agreeing to do the collective international bidding of other nations. By this legislation we give that obedience now, and in doing so I think we are making a significant move. Just as the question was asked in the United Kingdom parliament, we .might here ask whether other nations throughout the world are giving this power as well.
Of course, our position in Canada is this, that the world is but a shrunken ball of its former self, and here we are sandwiched between two great centres of power with competing ideals and whose efforts at closer collaboration have not always been successful. I

United Nations
think most of our people realize now that our property and our lives are perhaps more endangered by what happens from without than by what happens from within. It may be that between the last two wars when we took the isolationist stand we did we were greenhorns in diplomatic circles, but that does not entirely excuse us for what we did although it provides a pretty valuable lesson for what we should do at this time. Moreover, when we were taking the position we did we were travelling in pretty prominent isolationist company. I fancy that not only has Canada learned some lessons but the great republic to the south has learned some lessons too, and the events of very recent times have proven it, because the great republic to the south is now spending, not by the million but by the billion, on fire-ranging in various parts of the world in order to extinguish blazes which later might cost them as much if they actually got out of control, as they did in former times. Bearing that in mind, I suppose it is not to be wondered at that the Canadian people, the Canadian government and the Canadian parliament should find themselves digging deeper into the soil of world affairs than they ever did before.
I want to give this warning, Mr. Speaker. I wonder whether the Canadian people are keeping abreast of all this great movement into the international field which parliament and the government are taking.

speechtext: They have not a chance.

subtopic: POWERS OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL WITH RESPECT TO ARTICLE 41
speechtext:
My hon. friend says they have not a chance and perhaps he is right. He is right very often about a number of things. It seems to me essential that parliament and the government and public opinion should form one great team in Canada, for otherwise, if one gets ahead of the other, a disastrous reaction might conceivably set in. That is one of the things I am so anxious about. I am hopeful that we in parliament who have from time to time been representatives of this country in the united nations organization are carrying with us public opinion, because, after all, if this is to be a peace that will be permanent, it has to be a peace supported by the peoples of the world, or otherwise it can never be a permanent peace, as I hope and pray it will be.
The surrender of sovereignty, upon which one of my hon. friends spoke so eloquently this afternoon, is something which touches vitally the very life of our people. It is so easy to talk about the surrender of sovereignty 83166-220J
without knowing exactly what it means and without having experienced what it means. What our experience will be in the surrender of sovereignty is another matter for which perhaps I cannot answer. One sees examples of those who do not seem very anxious to give up their sovereignty, for I find, by the current issue of Newsweek, that the frankest pa-sage in Gromyko's speech was this-as you know. Mr. Speaker, Gromyko is the soviet representative on the security council:
The united nations is an organization of sovereign nations. The Soviet Union cannot agree that its national economy be made dependent on the will even of a majority of the control organ.
That, coming from one of the major powers in the world, is pretty difficult for us to understand, particularly in view of the fact that that great nation was one of those which had signed the charter in the first instance and is also protected by her veto on the security council.

subtopic: POWERS OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL WITH RESPECT TO ARTICLE 41
speechtext: Did the hon. member notice the word "economy" in there? Is any other nation prepared to surrender its economic sovereignty?

subtopic: POWERS OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL WITH RESPECT TO ARTICLE 41
speechtext:
My hon. friend is, I think, on an entirely different tack from the one I am taking. I am trying to indicate that the soviet itself is not reaching out with any great degree of eagerness and enthusiasm to allow other nations to direct its policy and tell it what it is going to do, and I would not have been at all surprised if Mr. Gromyko had made an even franker declaration if he were not speaking in public.
The other point I would make is this. This is our first bill which recognizes the fact that our sovereignty is to be surrendered in the interests of world peace and the united nations organization. This is the first bill which actually implements that partial surrender of sovereignty'. I think, too, that this bill means the gearing of ourselves to a new policy of more political surrender of national sovereignty to the united nations organization. It may be that many of us are not anxious to do that. It may be that some people look jealously upon our own rights so far as national sovereignty is concerned. But we signed the San Francisco charter with the overwhelming approval of the people as a whole. We signed what we are now purporting to implement so far as practical considerations are concerned.
One cannot look upon the economic sanctions end of our united nations work without thinking also of the collateral part, the military' sanctions. The military sanctions and the staff committee's report to the security coun-
United, Nations

cil have been one of the most disappointing and discouraging things that I have heard or read since I have had anything to do with the united nations itself. It is not setting up an international army, navy or air force. It does not purport to do that. The report in fact says that, because there are so many of the big powers which have a veto and can say no, there is no use in having a large army, navy or air force at all. In other words, we are not even to have an international police force. We are just going to have a nice easygoing little body of truant officers to make sure that the little boys throughout the world will not cause any trouble. But. Mr. Speaker, when did the little boys cause any trouble without the help of the big ones? You will not have a world war started until you get the big boys in there. You will have no global conflict and no world war until the big boys join in, although it might be started on the pretext of a little boy having done something.
I look askance, I look with grave disappointment at the fact that we are apparently to have a toothless- security council. That has many aspects that we do not always realize, because the whole question of national disarmament the world over is predicated on that very thing. There is not a single nation of the world that will disarm unless it is sure that its national security is to be guaranteed, and effectively guaranteed by somebody else or something else. If they cannot rely on anything more than a few truant officers in the security council there will never be any disarmament even on a minor scale in the world. That is one of the reasons why I look with such discouragement and disappointment upon the report of the military staff committee, because it might easily mean the beginning of an arms race again in the world, which most of us had hoped and prayed the united nations organization would obviate with its great structure for peace.
With respect to this particular bill, I must say that the United Kingdom are in a little different position from us. They have the veto so far as economic sanctions are concerned. We have none. Even if we are one of the non-permanent members of the security council, which we are not today, we shall not have any. Hon. members know what the veto means. I realize it is perhaps futile and hopeless to talk about it now. It was a compromise in the original instance, but you see what happens. You have five powers with the veto who can say that nothing will be done. That is what it means. Nothing will be done; you will not have economic sanction; you will not have international troops go into a country; in other words, they can paralyse the effort of

the united nations organization. Any one of the five can do that. What happens? Every little power cultivates a big power for a friend. Why would they not? It is the most natural thing in the world because, unless they have a big power for a friend, then the united nations organization might conceivably go in with their international force, small as it might conceivably be. With all that comes a gathering around with each one of the big five as a core. There is a gathering around of nations. What does that mean? That means the old days of power blocs in the world again. That is one of the things that we in Canada must watch very carefully.
I wish to make another observation that has nothing to do with military matters in the ordinary sense. When the San Francisco charter was signed I thought there were dangerous loopholes in it. One of the major loopholes is perhaps this. While in various parts of the charter we had provisions for economic sanctions, in other parts of the charter we provided for armed forces to stop aggression. But all the time we were talking about military aggression. The charter was silent on perhaps what has become the most modern, perhaps the strongest and most effective, certainly the most insidious, kind of aggression. The charter did not cover the question of ideological aggression at all.

subtopic: POWERS OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL WITH RESPECT TO ARTICLE 41
speechtext: Or industrial aggression.

subtopic: POWERS OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL WITH RESPECT TO ARTICLE 41
speechtext:
I shall be glad to have my hon. friend add to my speech because he can always make it better by doing so. But I wish to say that it would have been more to the point if some way could have been found whereby the united nations could apply some kind of sanctions to the ideological aggression which is so evident and so much abroad in the world today. It is not armed aggression, but it has the germs of provocation which, I hope, will not lead to armed aggression in the days that lie ahead, although there are certainly chances for that situation arising.
I hope that this bill will be carefully considered, not just on second reading. We are prepared to recommend second reading for the purpose of having it go before the external affairs committee. There are some parts of it that ought to go before that committee. Following the procedure which was adopted in the other house, I make this plea to the minister. In view of the fact that no evidence is available to us from the other place, the bill ought to be sent to a standing committee of the house. When that is done I hope that

United Nations
the government will give consideration to one or two matters which occurred to me as being important in connection with strengthening the bill. It is so important that I think the government ought to give some undertaking, so far as it can do so, that in serious cases, while parliament is sitting, the government will not unnecessarily avail itself of the wide and sweeping powers contained in the emergency legislation with which it is now clothed. I realize, and so does the government, that time may be of the essence so far as these matters are concerned. So far as I am personally concerned, I am not going to withhold from the government the right to act quickly if an emergency arises, because minutes and not hours may be the deciding factor with respect to sanctions. More than that, the government ought to do what the United Kingdom did, namely, not to wait for fifteen days or whatever the act calls for in regard to the time of tabling the order in council when parliament is sitting. If parliament is sitting the order in council should be laid on the table forthwith. That is what is done in the British house, and we could do no better than to follow the precedent that they have set.
The question of penalties ought to be thoroughly reviewed and considered. Those are matters that can be left to the good judgment of the standing committee on external affairs if the government sees fit to refer the bill to that body. In that committee we must see what practical factors are involved so far as the Canadian people are concerned. We must know that because it is essential. While some people may be carried off their feet by the onrushing winds of cloudy sentimentality, the nations of the world are beginning to be more realistic about the whole question of peace. We should make sure that we are applying common-sense Canadianism to world problems of today.
I also wish to mention what was referred to in one of the debates in the British house when a similar bill was before parliament there. It is something which we can take to heart ourselves. Let us not play with the question of the united nations and peace. So often-and I do not say this necessarily about any party or group in the house-we are somewhat hypocritical. Let us not be hypocritical about the whole question of peace and what it means. Very often -we talk one way and when it comes down to the hard cold facts we want to talk in another way. We cannot have our cake and eat it. I suggest that we have a policy of economic sanctions which is not the type of policy that the Canadian government repudiated in 1935, but a policy that, to use the words of a British statesman in the house when the debate was in progress, cannot be characterized as all bark and no bite.
I believe that many hon. members will be glad to endorse and approve this legislation, because Canada cannot stay out of a great structure of economic sanctions, since this nation must never leave itself in the position, so far as an offending nation is concerned, of being an international bootlegger in any sense of the term. That is not our role. It is not 1he kind of role Canada has played up to date or intends to play in the years that lie ahead.
Let me say this in conclusion. Either we mean business in this international fight to keep the peace, or we do not. If we do, then let us shoulder our full responsibility. If we do not, let us not be hypocritical but rather abandon the whole thing now.
I believe I speak for everyone in our party in this house when I say that I for one want Canada to pull her full weight and, having that definitely in mind, I will support this legislation for the reasons I mentioned a few moments ago.

subtopic: POWERS OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL WITH RESPECT TO ARTICLE 41
speechtext:
This piece of legislation is something we are obligated to adopt, and I think the suggestion of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), that the matter be considered by the committee on external affairs, is one which the government might well accept.
When I look at the charter of the united nations I realize to what an extent article 41 is intended to carry out the intention of the preamble:
We the peoples of the united nations, determined to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war, which twice in our lifetime has brought untold sorrow to mankind-
-obligate ourselves to do certain things. We obligate ourselves-
-to unite our strength to maintain international peace and security, and to ensure, by the acceptance of principles and the institution of methods, that armed force shall not be used, save in the common interest.
The article we are now discussing places in the hands of the security council a means whereby it is hoped that the subsequent use of armed force may be avoided. Consequently it is an article of the united nations charter which should command the support of all parties in this house.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the hon. member for Peel as he discussed the question of sovereignty. I do not regard our
United Nations

adherence to the united nations as in any way involving our surrender of sovereignty. To my mind, what it actually does is to extend our sovereignty far beyond our own borders, extending it into affairs where otherwise we might have no voice and might not be able to help to determine policy which might involve us in disastrous results in the years to come.
The very fact that we are a member of the united nations, though at the moment we are not a member of the security council, does give us an extension of our sovereignty over matters about which we would have no say and in which, at least, we would have no determining voice. And so this article 41 of me charter gives us a right to participate in measures that may be necessary in order to prevent the involvement of all other countries and our own in a worldwide war.
I do not think any of us in this house, whether we have seen the united nations in operation or not, and have followed the work of the security council and other organs of the united nations, can say that so far the organization has measured up to what those of us who were in San Francisco hoped it would attain. But in spite of all the criticisms that might be levelled against the united nations organization, one is inclined to ask the critics:	What do you suggest that could
take its place? That is the crucial question. What is there that could be 'devised which at this moment would take it place?
I hope that one day we may reach the stage foreshadowed by the prophets of old when we may beat our swords into ploughshares, when the lion may lie down with the lamb, and when we may live together as a great brotherhood, under some kind of federation or parliament of man. But the parliament of man is a long way off. I believe it is possible through an organization, even as we have set it up at the present time, to look forward to its ending the possibility of armed conflict among the peoples. I say, armed conflict, because I agree with the hon. member for Peel that there are two kinds of struggle. There is also the ideological struggle, but I would say to him that I know of no way in which it would be possible to prevent the flow of ideas across the world, which are at the root of the ideological struggle; and my reliance, as far a,s the ideological struggle is concerned, is upon the belief that the democratic way, democratic methods of self-government, will enable our people to do all those things which are necessary to improve our standards of living, and so on, so that ultimately the ideology of freedom, in the political and in

the economic sphere, will be attained and safeguarded because of its rightness and its power.
May I ask that you call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.
