subtopic: POWERS OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL WITH RESPECT TO ARTICLE 41
speechtext:
Before six o'clock, I was discussing article 41 of the charter of the united nations, and had remarked that we could not draw a curtain across the world and prevent ideas from flowing in various directions; nor should we seek to do so. I know the feeling of the various delegates who were present at the meeting of the united nations in New York last autumn, and before that in London and San Francisco, was the feeling expressed by Mrs. Roosevelt on one occasion, when she said of her work on the economic and social council that it was the most exasperating thing in the world.
We know we have to arrive at understandings with the country that in the last twenty-five years has emerged as a great world power. I refer to Russia. They do not understand our approach to the problems which confront the world, nor do we understand their approach. I sometimes think we could learn a lesson from our own history. After all, for years they were more or less outlawed among the nations, and the treatment we accorded them between the wars accounts in no small measure for the distrust and suspicion they now feel with regard to us. Except for some of their top leaders, and incidentally very few of them, none of the Russians has had any close contact either with the outside world or with the ideas we represent. I think we have to bear in mind that they came into power after a revolution

United Nations
which they had fomented by all possible means, including widespread conspiracy. If we know the history of revolutions I think we shall realize that for a period after a revolution the ideas which brought it about and the methods by which the revolution was made successful are the methods that follow a revolution. Even in our own British history, if you go back to the Stuart period you find the overthrow of Charles; Cromwell; then the restoration; the coming of James; the overthrow of James, and so on. All during that period you find a history of intolerance that seems to be common to revolutionary and post-revolutionary periods. Similar experiences, to a degree, followed the French revolution. And we have to bear in mind that on the foundation which was built up prior to and following the revolution is imposed a philosophy of Marxism, applied to the Russian situation. I think all this accounts for a great many of the difficulties with which the world is faced today. After all, the Soviet Union is a young nation in the field of the world diplomacy, and her leaders have not had the experience and training the leaders of the western nations have had. So I feel keenly that, while we must stand firmly by our democratic principles and traditions, we should endeavour at all times and everywhere to understand the background of the people with whom we are trying to come to an understanding at the present time. It seems to me, if we can do that, we shall be moving a long way toward a better understanding in the world.
This article 41 of the charter gives the security council certain powers, including the power to take measures exclusive of war, and commits us to participation in those measures. I hope we shall never have to use any of the enforcement measures provided in the charter. We may have to do so, but I hope not. In any event, I think it is wise, considering the state in which the world is now, that we should be properly prepared to do whatever may be necessary in order to promote peace, first, and prevent war if war is threatened, and to put down aggression should aggression occur. I sometimes think the people of today are unaware of the difficulty which faces mankind, and the threat which overshadows the world. When we think of the new weapons of war, and particularly the atomic weapons, we begin to realize that if war did come there are only two countries which conceivably could participate in such a war. Those nations are, of course, the United States and Russia; and neither, except for destroying the centres of population of the other, could achieve a successful invasion or the conquest of the
other. Perhaps that realization on the part of both may be one of the factors which will enable the world to preserve peace. No one can gain from the type of war that will come if the united nations organization fails. As I said this afternoon, while we may be some distance from any form of world government, world government must come if we are to have universal peace some time. I do not expect that will come in my lifetime or in the lifetime of hon. members of this House of Commons, though we strive to that end, but at least we have, within the united nations, an organization which may be a foundation upon which permanent peace can be built.
As far as Canada's part in this political and ideological struggle is concerned, I think we should take the middle view, the view that is being taken by the western European people and the people of Great Britain; that, instead of inflaming public opinion against the United States on the one hand or against Russia on the other, we should do all we can -and I think Canada can do a great deal- to bring about an understanding between these two great powers and among the united nations. As I said once before in the house, I was pleased that the head of the Canadian delegation, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent), was the first delegate at New York, at the second part of the first session of the assembly, to draw to the attention of the assembled nations the fact that we had not yet laid the foundations of security enforcement, if I may put it in that way; for Canada, and particularly those nations which are not the so-called great nations, have a tremendous stake in seeing to it that the security council operates without war.
As the leader of our delegation said in New York, unless we can devote to the building of homes and the improvement of the conditions of life of our people in our countries the amount we shall be compelled to devote for defensive purposes, and unless we are able to make this charter effective, we cannot in the days to come improve our standard of living as we would like to improve it. Instead of, as our people thought as they were fighting the war, and when the war ended, our being on the threshold of a newer and better age, we may sink down into the depths of despair and misery. That will be the result, unless we can make this organization work.
So I wanted to say tonight that we must try to bring about better understanding among nations, and particularly between the two giants which emerged from this war. I know it is exceedingly difficult to get our point of view into the Soviet Union; and
United Nations

sometimes I feel that perhaps the point of view of the Soviet union is not always placed accurately before our own people. One had only to be at those conferences to realize that very often the reports published, and particularly those in some sections of the United States press, with respect to discussions which took place in the various committees and the assembly gave a most distorted picture of what actually occurred in the discussions.
So far as the article and the bill before us are concerned, let me say that we support the bill because we believe it is another step in the promotion of peace and in Canada's support of the only organization to which we can look at this time for the preservation of peace in the world.
And I say to those critics of the united nations, and of the united nations charter, that when they criticize they should be prepared to say what they have to offer the world in its place. If there is nothing else, then it seems to me the best thing to do is to support what we have. It may not be as effective as we would like it to be; nevertheless I believe it is a step forward. Though it may be a difficult step, and may sometimes appear to a great many people, a feeble step, yet it is a step we ourselves should take with the rest of the world.
Therefore I say, Mr. Speaker, that we support the second reading of the bill.
Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River): Mr. Speaker, I find it difficult to imagine all the things which are involved or which might be involved in Bill No. 132. What I find considerably more important, and perhaps embarrassing, is that I have not as yet been able to envision all the purposes for which the provisions of the bill might be used. I consider it my duty to find out these things before I say whether I will support the bill or not. There are implications in it which I certainly do not like. It may be that my fears are not well founded, but that can be known only after I have given the bill the most thorough investigation.
I will challenge anybody who has not been a participant in the sessions of the united nations to say at this stage just what is implied in the provisions of the bill.

subtopic: POWERS OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL WITH RESPECT TO ARTICLE 41
speechtext: Even they cannot do it.

subtopic: POWERS OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL WITH RESPECT TO ARTICLE 41
speechtext:
I am afraid I must agree with what the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) has said. Many things have been said in this debate-and it has been short, it is true-about peace, and about putting teeth
[Mr. ColdweJl.l
into international legislation to ensure peace.
I listened with keen attention to the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) and also to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell).
I must say that the group which I represent, and for which I certainly am speaking at this time, will take second place to no group in its desire for world peace. We are sincere in our desire for that condition. But I must say further that we take a realistic position with respect to the means by which peace shall be achieved.
Let me remind the house that peace does not stem from statutes, from sanctions exercised upon people, or from coercion. Peace resides in and springs from the hearts of men. The will to peace has to be cultivated in the hearts of men. The only satisfactory condition for world peace is that which can be found in finding out, by careful study and investigation what the causes of war are, and then removing them at the earliest possible time.
I would feel much happier about the united nations and the work it has done if I could have seen it giving much more of its time to a study of the causes of war, instead of watching it giving its undivided attention to other aspects of international relations such as force or sanctions, or ways of divesting nations of their sovereignty-which, in itself, I remind hon. members, is very often a cause of war.
I believe that the provisions of Bill No. 132 may have such far-reaching results that we, as responsible representatives of the people, should exercise the greatest care in becoming thoroughly informed about it, and about what it provides for. Further than that, I think we should do everything we can to see that the Canadian people are made fully aware of its implications.
I know there is widespread anxiety not only here in Canada but elsewhere in the world about the effectiveness of the united nations, about whether or not the united nations will be able to achieve what it set out to achieve, namely world peace. I find, as I talk to people wherever I go, that they have not much knowledge about it; they have not much information.
I recall that back in 1945 when the house was debating the united nations charter, and whether parliament should approve Canada's participation in the united nations, I pointed out what I believed were some of the dangers and some of the weaknesses in the charter. I suggested then that the only way the united nations could possibly be successful would be to have the undivided support of the people, not only of this country, but of every other

United Nations
country in the world participating in it. I suggested at that time that one means of mobilizing that support would be by means of the radio. In Canada we had the network of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation stretching across Canada, and we should have given over that radio network every bit of information it was possible to gather about the united nations, so as to allow the people to measure its possibilities, to judge of it and to get to understand it. I say once more that the most effective motive force for any organization designed to bring about world peace, such as the united nations, must come from the awakened conscience of the people. We cannot expect to impose peace by sanction or statute; it must come out of the people. I am concerned about getting information to the people, and I suggest that one of the best ways of informing the public is to have this bill go before the standing committee on external affairs. I support that suggestion whole-heartedly. I spoke to the minister about it the other day and he suggested he would give it consideration. I hope he has given it that consideration and will be ready to move that the bill be sent to the committee where we can examine witnesses, where representatives of the press can be present to give publicity to the information that may be brought out.
I understand that this bill was referred to the standing committee on external affairs in the other place but I searched everywhere for the proceedings of that committee and I was very much disappointed to find that such an important measure should be discussed and investigated without any record of the committee's proceedings being kept. I voice this in criticism of that other place. If they are to justify their existence surely it is their responsibility to provide a record of their proceedings, especially in connection with a matter of such importance as this bill and others that originate in that place and are sent here for our consideration. I believe I speak for my group when I say that we want to know all that it is possible to know about the bill and its implications before we can say whether or not we will support it. I have serious doubts as to whether it does not inn afoul of provincial rights, and I believe the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) suggested the same fears. I wonder if the minister, when he is making his rebuttal, will set our minds at rest on that point? This and many other questions ought to be fully investigated before hon. members attempt to express their judgment on the bill. Therefore I suggest
that- the Secretary of State for External Affairs give us the assurance that it will be sent to the committee on external affairs.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was hopeful that we would hear tonight a real formula for peace when the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Coldwell) said that we should beat our swords into ploughshares and our spears into pruning hooks. He should have gone on and given us a real formula for peace, but he did not. I am not one who claims that you can have an abiding peace on an economic and social security foundation, because foundations of that kind change with the country in which you live. If the leader of the C.C.F. had gone on a little farther with his quoting of Isaiah he would have found that even away back in Isaiah's time it was found that the foundation for the cure of war was to be found in the Prince of Peace. As Paul said, other foundations can no man lay. You can have all the money you could possibly use; you can have all the things you could possibly be surrounded with, but if you have not the source of peace in the individual heart you are not going to have peace in the nation. You can have that peace only by building on the one foundation. When the nations of the world come to that understanding, then we shall have peace at home and we shall have peace abroad.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the house finishes with this matter, there are several things which I consider it my duty to bring to the attention of the house. The hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) asked a question which I believe had a considerable effect upon hon. members. He asked:	What have
we to put in the place of the united nations? I should like to be granted the indulgence of the house for a while to say something concerning that matter. I think the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) put his finger on the root of the whole situation. I do not recall his exact words, but the thought I got from them was this:	It is just as
foolish to try to build an edifice to guarantee the peace of the world on unsound, unstable and unsatisfactory foundations economically and socially as it would be to try to build a New York sky-scraper on a bed of quicksand. The economic and social foundations which exist among men today are just as unstable and treacherous as a bed of quicksand. The objection which I have taken to this whole united nations situation since early 1945 has been based on the ground that no adequate attention has been given to these economic and social foundations
United Nations

which are so treacherous and which have caused such terrible trouble in the world during the last forty years.
I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to some matters which are very serious. Some of the material which I propose to present to the house tonight I have had in my hands for a year and a half. I have been doubtful as to whether or not I should put it on Hansard', but I have a feeling that the time has come to put some of this important material on the record so that it can be considered when this bill is being considered. This bill is supposed to be a measure to strengthen the united nations, the object being to enable the world to have peace. Let us examine the whole thing in the light of some of these facts.
First, as the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) said, let us find the cause of war. We do not need to go back any farther than the war from which we have just emerged. What caused that war? I am going into this in an effort to find out whether the thing we have established as the united nations has even a ghost's chance of dealing with the cause of war and preventing war. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar both expressed dissatisfaction with what has happened as regards the united nations up to the present time. There is a fundamental reason for the failure of that organization.
Why is Russia taking such a strong stand in the whole matter of the united nations? I am afraid it is done for two reasons. In the first place, the Russians seem to know more about essential fundamentals in trade than we seem to be able to get through our heads. Next, the Russians are not afraid to tell the truth and face the facts when they know them, and it seems to me that a good many of our people are afraid to tell the truth and face the facts.
What caused world war II? Let me turn to what brought Japan and the United States into conflict in the last world war. I shall have to refer to some documents to show what brought them to clash, but briefly I would say it was the fact that the United States insisted that the most favoured nation clause should apply to herself and Japan. Japan knew that if the most favoured nation clause were established as a fundamental basis for trade relations between herself and the LTnited States, the economic existence of Japan would be rendered an impossibility; and so they fought. I believe I can adduce evidence which will satisfy every hon. member, or at least it will give him food for thought. I turn, first of all, to the document of November 
26, 1941, a statement by Cordell Hull to the Japanese ambassador while they were negotiating. There is every indication in the words which were used that the Japanese were struggling even at that late date to avoid the calamity of war. I read from clause 4 of section 1 of the document-as usual the people who know all about these things are not listening. The second paragraph of the clause reads:
The government of Japan-
It is the United States speaking.
-and the government of the United States have agreed that toward eliminating chronic political instability, preventing recurrent economic collapse, and providing a basis for peace, they will actively support and practically apply the following principles in their economic relations with each other and with other nations and peoples:
(1)	The principle of non-discrimination in international commercial relations.
(2)	The principle of international economic cooperation and abolition of extreme nationalism as expressed in excessive trade restrictions.
(3)	The principle of non-discriminatory access by all nations to raw material supplies.
(4)	The principle of full protection of the interests of consuming countries and populations as regards the operation of international commodity agreements.
(5)	The principle of establishment of such institutions and arrangements of international finance-
Think of Bretton Woods!
-as may lend aid to the essential enterprises and the continuous development of all countries and may permit payments through processes of trade consonant with the welfare of all countries.
May I just point out to the members of the house how familiar those words sound in our ears-in our ears who have read the Dumbarton Oaks conference report and the Bretton Woods conference report. What the United States was insisting on in effect was the establishment practically of those two sets of proposals; and it was because Japan could not possibly accept those conditions that she resisted even by war.
Now I quote a little further on from the same document, clause 6 of section 2:
The government of the United States and the government of Japan will enter into negotiations for the conclusion between the United States and Japan of a trade agreement, based upon reciprocal most-favoured-nation treatment and reduction of trade barriers by both countries, including an undertaking by the United States to bind raw silk on the free list.
Now, Mr. Speaker and hon. members, it stands out as clear as the sun in a cloudless sky that what the United States insisted on was the most favoured nation clause. Have

you heard any word from the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) concerning that matter? Have you heard a single word from the member for Peel (Mr. Gray-don) concerning that matter? Have you heard a single word from any member of the Liberal party concerning that matter? Why is it there has been no discussion in this house of the cause of the last war? Can you imagine any hon. member of this house who is a medical doctor undertaking to cure a disease before he diagnoses the cause?

We in this house and apparently in all the legislatures in all parts of the British commonwealth have been setting about to find a cure for the ills that afflict this generation and which resulted in two wars without giving any attention to the cause. No wonder the united nations arrangement is a disappointment-no wonder! And now it is proposed that this house put through a measure which is supposed to put teeth into the security council, which is to be guided in its thinking and its operations in this world by a group of men who apparently know nothing whatsoever about the causes of war and are in no way disposed to remove those causes, people apparently who are intent upon trying to deal with symptoms instead of the causes of disease.
I should like to say just a word about the people m the other place. I wanted to rise and ask the hon. member for Peel a question this afternoon while he was speaking, but I feared I might throw him off his line' of thought. I wanted to ask him this question: Where did he suppose the other place got this measure we now are discussing? Where did it come from? Did some member of the other place draft this bill? Who put it into the hands of the members in the other place? And who was the member in the other place who sponsored this bill and supported it? No wonder the hearings of the committee that investigated this bill were never printed! And here we are sitting here and paying no attention to important matters like that. Where was this bill drafted-in Canada or in the United States? That is important. The hon. member for Peel this afternoon almost let the cat out of the bag when he said that certain senators "were able to get certain changes." This bill was supposed to originate with the members of the other place. Yet the members of the other place had to struggle apparently to get changes in the bill! Surely the members of this house are not going to go into this thing with their eyes closed! Surely

there is the handwriting on the wall! Surely there is ample cause for suspicion and anxiety in a procedure like that!
Let me go forward with the cause of world war II. I come now to what the Japanese say, just to show whether what I have indicated, was actually the cause of the war. Here is the reply which the Japanese ambassador put into the hands of the United States government. I am quoting from subclause 1 of clause 4 of the document put into the hands of the United States government at 2.20 p.m. on December 7, 1941:
The American government advocates in the name of world peace those principles favourable to it and urges upon the Japanese government the acceptance thereof. The peace of the world may be brought about only by discovering a mutually acceptable formula through recognition of the reality of the situation and mutual appreciation of one another's position. An attitude such as ignores realities and imposes one's selfish views upon others will scarcely serve the purpose of facilitating the consummation of negotiations.
That is so beautifully put, so humbly put, so clearly and so tersely put, that it is like a cry of anguish,

May I turn now to the question of what to do instead of having the united nations organization. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar despairs about it. He seems to think that if it fails we shall have the atomic bomb on us, and all the other horrible things he fears. Well, in the last war we could have used gas and utterly destroyed the world, but we did not; we could have waged bacterial warfare and utterly destroyed mankind, but we did not. I presume in the next world war we shall have tile atomic bomb, which could be used then to destroy the peoples of the world, but we shall not use it. People have too much fun fighting and killing one another to kill themselves off completely. They will not do that. The hon. member need not despair so much. If, however, the fundamental causes of war are not removed, men will fight, no matter what they fight with, whether it be atomic bombs or their teeth or fingernails, because they will have to fight in order to live.
The hon. member asks what we could do to replace the U.N.O. The other night I made a speech on this question. I know I shall not be allowed to read from it now, but I would refer hon. members to the remarks I made on. May 16. as recorded at page 3170 of Hansard, where I answered that question in the speech I then made. I pointed out that it would be perfectly feasible to organize the nations of good will in the world under an organization like the British commonwealth, in which every nation has its sovereignty, but in which every nation, because of a common purpose and understanding, will stand together with the rest in order to accomplish great ends.

United Nations
There is not a nation in the world, as far as I know, that would not join such an organization if the matter were put plainly before it. As I pointed out the other night, this is the kind of thing that Anthony Eden advised. Let us have an organization built upon a blueprint after the fashion of the British commonwealth. He certainly did not imply any support of the monstrous organization that was erected in the united nations organization, or such a horrible engine as the security council, which threatens to deprive the nations of their sovereignty.
If we have an organization like the British commonwealth, which we can have if we will, and then adopt the nine principles which I advocated the other night, some of them too far advanced for many members of the house to accept, but wThich nevertheless will be found important and sound, then we shall have an alternative.
Before I go into that, however, I should like to point out for the information of hon. members-and I believe all hon. members will agree with me-that the fundamental and inevitable cause of war is economic, and the fundamental, economic cause is the fact that, as nations trade, some of them fall into adverse trade balances and debt to others for the reason that they cannot keep their people from buying more goods from those other nations than those other nations will buy from them. We in Canada are witnessing that process right at the present time, even with our vast resources around us. What, then, must be the pathetic condition of a nation like Belgium, or Holland, or Czechoslovakia, or Yugoslavia when it undertakes to protect its economy? What must have been the position of Italy, with its
47.000.	000 people on their barren slopes. What must have been the position of Hitler with
66.000.	000 crowded in an area not one-third as large as Ontario. The fear of an adverse trade balance was insistent, that and the establishment of unrepayable international debt, debt that can be repaid only in goods.
Take Canada as an illustration. We fall into debt to the United States, and we cannot pay because the United States will not accept our goods, which is the only means we have of repaying the debt. They put up tariff barriers, establish quotas, and by several other means prevent us from paying, which means that they put us into a state of unrepayable debt. When nations suffer that sort of thing they cannot avoid war. It is either war or utter national economic destruction. They prefer the war. There we have the fundamental cause of wars. Mr. Speaker, I shall keep the house from coming to the question for only a few minutes, but in view of the fact that the united nations has been referred to as an iniquitous organization I feel that something else ought to be said before this debate closes. I for one am aware of the fact that the united nations structure as it now stands has certain shortcomings, that improvements are needed, and it is also true, as the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) has said, that we should do everything we can to muster popular support for this people's organization. But it must be pointed out that the world would be in a sorry state if there were not some hope in the united nations. The fact is that for all its shortcomings it is grappling with some of the fundamental problems of war and peace. I want to refer in one sentence to the fact that an integral part of the united nations set-up is the economic and social council which is dealing with these fundamental problems.
It seems to me that the principle of the bill before us is so clear that there ought not to have been any necessity for arguing the point, nor should there have been the straying that has been evident during the course of this debate. We are not debating at this time the charter of the united nations. That charter has already been agreed to by some fifty-five nations, members of the organization, and not only has Canada signed the charter, but its signature has been approved by a unanimous vote by both houses of parliament. I submit, therefore, that we are not 
now arguing the merits of the charter nor the merits of article 41. One of the articles in that charter is article 25, which reads:
The members of the united nations agree to accept and carry out the decisions of the security council in accordance with the present charter.
The principle of the bill before us is simply this: Is this parliament prepared to give the government of the day the necessary constitutional power to carry out a commitment we have already made? In the interests of international organization, in the interests of the wider sovereignty it provides, in the interests of world peace, I am glad that the government of the day has brought this measure before us, and I believe that it should receive the unanimous support of the house.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext: I made a long statement on the resolution.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the bill before us deals with two main principles. One is the. change from three commissioners to one commissioner and two deputies, and the other is to include the words "prison reformatories" in the term "penitentiaries".
No doubt this bill is designed to implement a recent decision of the government, presumably on the recommendation of the commissioner as it appears in his report which was tabled during the present session. I should like to quote from pages 8 and 9 of that report of the. commissioner, General R. B. Gibson. He says:
(a)	The royal commission proposed the appointment of a prison commission composed of three members to administer the penal system of Canada responsible directly to the Minis-

Penitentiary Act
ter of Justice. It is evident that in making this recommendation the royal commission had in mind its further recommendation that the federal government take over the administration of all the prisons in Canada, thus centralizing the control of the Canadian penal system under the government of Canada. As will be stated later, it is not 5ret considered practicable to give effect to this recommendation and the government has recently decided that for the present it is preferable to entrust the administration of the penitentiaries of Canada to a single commissioner assisted by two deputy commissioners, with a headquarters organization consisting of the inspectors and staff of the present penitentiaries branch, the inspectors being reclassified as assistant commissioners.
(b)	It is proposed that one deputy commissioner will be primarily charged with the selection. training, assessment and further reconstruction of the staffs of the penitentiaries and with the organization and supervision of a training school for penitentiary officers. He will also be responsible for the supervision and development of the educational facilities in the institutions under the control of the dominion government.
(cl It is proposed that the second deputy commissioner will be primarily charged with supervision and development of the medical and psychiatric services, physical training and recreational facilities as well as the development of research and statistics to assess the adenuacy and results of present and proposed methods of correctional treatment.
While the commissioner's report presumes . to deal with implementing the recommendations of the royal commission presided over by Mr. Justice Archambault, there is a change from three commissioners to one commissioner, and therefore it is a serious departure from the recommendations of the Archambault commission. As I understand the situation, the recommendation for a three-man commission was adopted in the enactment of chapter 6 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1939, and in enacting this measure, which is the present Penitentiary Act, which by the way with the exception of one or two sections has not yet been proclaimed, the main principle was the appointment of a three-man commission. I read from the debates of the House of Commons of 1939, at page 1472 of Hansard, where the then minister of justice, the Right Hon. Mr. Lapointe, introduced the resolution preceding that legislation and reading as follows:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to establish a commission with power under the Minister of Justice, to administer, control and manage the penitentiaries; to provide for salaries of the commissioners and assistant commissioners: and, generally, to repeal and reenact with consequential amendments the Penitentiary Act.
Later on, in explanation of his resolution, the then minister of justice said:
It will be-
That is the new act.
-the Penitentiary Act substantially as it is today in the statute, except that it provides for the establishment of a commission of three to replace the superintendent of penitentiaries.
The commission to be appointed was, I presume, to be a commission of three men and decisions were to be made by three commissioners. In the case of a disagreement I presume the majority would prevail. The new enactment before us this evening sets aside this important principle, and if the new enactment were adopted the commission would consist of just one commissioner and two deputy commissioners, who would simply obey the orders of the commissioner and perform the duties assigned by him. I think this is a grievous mistake which I should like the Minister of Justice to reconsider. There is no question that three men are better than one, speaking generally; but particularly in this case it is of the utmost importance that the decisions should not be just the opinions of one man.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext: Would the hon. member say that fifteen would be better than three?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
Not necessarily. We deal here with human beings who, it is true, have run foul of the law. They are still human beings and many factors must be considered in their treatment, both as to punishment and as to their rehabilitation.
I have no criticism to offer of General Gibson's appointment. I understand and I have heard that he is an energetic and capable person; but, Mr. Speaker, is it not strange that when the appointment is made of a superintendent or of any other high official under the Penitentiary Act and in the penitentiary service we cannot think of anyone except a military man. From the results of their administration of penitentiaries prior to the Archambault report, they have not exactly covered themselves with glory, as the report of the Archambault commission would indicate. Could not the minister think of some penologist or some similar expert to head the proposed commission or at least to be a member of it? I presume that a military man was picked because we have to have discipline in our penal institutions and military men are naturally reputed to be good disciplinarians. While I do not admit that discipline, at least as I understand the term, is the main factor in the treatment of our prisoners, yet it is an important one. I have no objection to a military man being one of the three members of the commission with the other two being trained in penology, psychology, criminology, social service or other similar branches of knowledge.
Penitentiary Act

This matter was brought up in the debate in 1939, and the then minister of justice seemed to have the same idea. I quote from his remarks at page 1477 of Hansard of 1939. This is what the then minister of justice said:
I can assure my hon. friend that these men will not be selected because of political affiliations. We will try to have men who are expert in this work. It has been urged for some time that there should be a medical man on the staff of the penitentiaries, an expert in mental diseases and that sort of thing. The idea is to have three men at the head of our penal system whose names and abilities will be a guarantee to the people of Canada that this very important branch of the administration is being looked after properly.
I think that is what the Arehambault commission had principally in mind when it so strongly recommended the appointment of a three-man commission. To emphasize this point, let me quote from the Arehambault report at pages 342 and 343. This is what the Arehambault. commission has to say:
In our present system the problem of penal administration is too large in scope and too serious in results to be left in the hands of one man. It is noteworthy, as a matter of record, that Canada is practically the only country where the penal system is not administered by some kind of commission or board.
I may say that this same paragraph was also quoted by the then minister of justice in 1939 in support of his resolution at that time. I continue to quote from the Archam-bault report:
In Great Britain, the prison commission is composed of a chairman and, two other commissioners. one administrative and the other medical, and is reenforced by four assistant commissioners, one of whom acts as secretary.
Then on page 343:
Under this system the continuity of policy can be maintained and the control of prisons, though subject to the will of parliament, is divorced from the changing views of party policy. Each member of the commission is responsible for his own share of the work of the department. Differences of opinion may arise in the course of the commission's discussions but. to date, it has not been found necessary on any occasion to bring a question to a vote for settlement.
The act of 1939 differs very little from the old Penitentiary Act, being chapter 154 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927. Its important difference is the setting up of the commission in the place of the one superintendent. This important change is now to be discarded and the old method of a one man czar to administer our penal institutions is to be readopted. The main difference is that, instead of calling him a superintendent, we shall now call him a commissioner. I am 
afraid that I cannot give my support to a step which, I believe, is a retreat from a former more advanced policy.
When I first read General Gibson's report my reaction was favourable, but when I had more time for study any favourable impression was soon dissipated. I have not the time to go fully into every phase of the report about which I might offer criticism or disagreement, but I shall confine myself to efforts in making suggestions or recommendations as to how we might accomplish or make a start in unifying our penal system.
When General Gibson says, as I quoted a few moments ago-
It is evident that in recommending the three-man commission tire royal commission had in mind its further recommendation that the federal government take over the administration of all prisons in Canada thus centralizing the control of the Canadian penal system under the government of Canada.
-I wish with great respect to differ from the general in that regard. The three-man commission was recommended, irrespective of whether or not we had a unified or centralized penal system throughout Canada.
The last paragraph of that section of the royal commission's report dealing with the recommendation of the three-man commission reads as follows, and may be found on page 344 of the report:
The prison commission, as recommended, would perform the functions now performed by the superintendent and three inspectors. It would have power to appoint staffs, and would act as a central parole board. The members should be removable only for cause.
I therefore maintain that the recommendations are not interdependent. What does the commissioner say about the unification of the penal system? I quote from his report on pages 14 and 15:
(a)	The royal commission recommended that the Canadian penal system should be centralized under the control of the government of Canada, with the federal authorities taking charge of all the prisons in Canada, the provinces retaining only a sufficient number to provide for offenders against provincial statutes, prisoners on remand, and those serving short sentences.
(b)	Under the British North America Act legislative authority for the establishment, maintenance and management of penitentiaries is assigned to the parliament of Canada, whereas the provincial legislatures have authority to make laws in relations to the establishment, maintenance and management of public and reformatory prisons in and for the province. It thus appears that while the provincial legislatures alone have legislative authority to provide for reformatory institutions in and for their respective provinces, the establishment or acquisition of reformatory institutions with dominion wide scope is not excluded from the sphere of the government of Canada.

Penitentiary Act
(c)	The royal commission suggested that centralization night be accomplished by two methods:
(i)	by amending the criminal code, the Penitentiary Act and the Prisons and Reformatories Act to change the minimum term for which a convicted person may be sentenced to a penitentiary to a period of less than two years; or
(ii)	by an agreement being made between the dominion and the provinces for the former to take over the administration of provincial penal institutions, in order that persons committed to prison for terms of less than two years might be committed to federal institutions.
(d)	It is evident that in the present state of the law any comprehensive change in the control of penal institutions can only be reached by agreement between the dominion and provincial governments.
While I cannot wholly concur in the conclusions of the commissioner as set forth in that last sentence, what has he done to see whether agreement between the dominion and provincial governments can be reached?
On page 3 of the report he speaks of many visits to provincial institutions, and informal discussions with provincial officials on matters of penal administration and policy, but the report is silent as to whether these discussions pertained to a unified system, and what were the reactions of the provinces, or what were their respective views on the matter?
There is a movement of reform in many of the provinces today, and one would think the provinces would be only too willing to cooperate with the dominion. Indeed, one paragraph on page 11 of the report seems to indicate that the maritime provinces are only too anxious to cooperate. I quote from page 11 of Commissioner Gibson's report:
In the maritime provinces there is at present nothing between the county gaols and the penitentiary at Dorchester, New Brunswick. The royal commission recommended the establishment of a central prison farm for the maritime provinces to afford better facilities for the confinement and reformation of prisoners serving sentences of less than two years than are available in the county gaols. This proposal is now under discussion with the provinces, who have suggested that such an institution be operated on their behalf by the dominion government, [f satisfactory arrangements can be made for ihe establishment of such an institution, with senarate facilities for dealing with young offenders, it will provide improved facilities for the classification and segregation of offenders in the maritime provinces.
I will say that if the provinces are in that mood, if the other provinces feel the same as the maritime provinces-and I have reason to believe they do-we should proceed along those lines immediately and quit worrying about the British North America Act.

I admit that, but I think we can make an immediate start such as the proposed action in the maritimes and follow it up with other provinces which might be willing to cooperate. The report contains come notable proposals on segregation and treatment of young offenders, and it will be of interest to quote some sections. First, I would refer to page 10, paragraph (b):
As a first step in developing a plan of segregation, it is proposed to provide in Kingston penitentiary in the east and in Manitoba penitentiary in the west for the detention of incorrigible and intractable prisoners whose conduct and anti-social attitude makes it desirable to separate them from the normal prison population in other institutions.
I commend this. Later on, on the same page, in paragraph (d) I quote:
It is proposed to develop Collin's Bay penitentiary in the east and Saskatchewan penitentiary in the west as institutions for the treatment of young convicts and the reformable type of prisoner.
I also endorse this. Then on the same page, in paragraph (e):
The situation in the province of Quebec must be dealt with as a separate problem because of the difficulty and undesirability of transferring persons who speak the French language to institutions staffed by English-speaking personnel.

At present St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary is filled to its capacity of 1,100 and contains in its population some 165 young convicts under the age of 21 years. A population of 1,100 is too large to be handled efficiently. Your commissioner therefore recommends that authority be obtained for the establishment of a new institution in the province of Quebec separate from St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, and that this institution be of the reformatory type, to which could be transferred youthful and reformable offenders sentenced to terms of two years or more in the province of Quebec. It is anticipated that the principles of the Borstal system may be applied to this institution.
While all this is not yet according to the Borstal system, nor is it satisfactory segregation, it is, in m}T opinion, at least a start, especially in Quebec and in the maritimes, where new institutions are recommended to be set up. Collin's Bay and the penitentiary in Saskatchewan are to be a sort of quasi-Borstal system, but they will always retain the character and especially the reputation of grim prisons, and after some start which we might make we shall have to instal the Borstal system throughout Canada. Indeed, the same sort of experiment with regard to the special treatment of young offenders has been tried at Collin's Bay, and the superintendent reports some pleasing results in the last report with regard to the special treatment of prisoners in that institution. On page 7 of the penitentiaries report there is an interesting table. 1 shall quote only the last two years. It is a table giving the number of prisoners discharged from Collin's Bay since 1930 and shows the number of those who have been reconvicted. There has been a considerable improvement in the last two years. In 1943-44 the total discharged were 128 and the total reconvicted were 28. In 1944-45 the total discharged were 122 and the total reconvicted were only 16. The superintendent goes on to make this comment thereon:
One thousand four hundred and eleven convicts out of 1,779 being apparently reformed and leading a normal citizen's life, is, I submit, a most interesting achievement. As already stated, the percentage of the repeaters, as far as penitentiary sentences are concerned, is 20-68. This satisfactory result is mainly due, and this must be emphasized, to the fact that those convicts while serving sentence at Collin's Bay penitentiary, were not contaminated by hardened recidivists, nor were they in contact with any habitual offender who through the years has learned "all the tricks of the trade" and who boasts of his criminal career.
The results of this experiment are encouraging, especially in the last few years, as I have pointed out, and I trust that this will be followed up and continued, but not at the expense of the other experiments which the commissioner has or should have in view and which I have already mentioned. However, as far as

statistics go, the situation in Collin's Bay seems' to be the one bright spot. I do not wish to go into tables of statistics and comparisons with other countries, but the latest statistics available to me show that, while non-indictable or minor offences have declined during the war years, there was no such decline in connection with indictable or major offences, and they are still on the up-grade. From 397 per 100,000 population in 1942 to 410 per 100,000 population in 1944-these are the latest figures available to me. Convictions of young offenders are still worse. Convictions of young offenders between the ages of sixteen and twenty-one rose from 773 per 100,000 population in 1942 to 1,022 per 100,000 in 1944. That is for major indictable offences, which shows that the situation is still serious.
The superintendent's report deserves the careful consideration of all hon. members and contains an interesting summary of the reports of chaplains of the penitentiaries. They were instructed to analyse the causes which led certain classes of convicts to the penitentiaiy. I wish to quote the case of two boys, cited in the report of the superintendent at page 50. This report was compiled by one of the penitentiary chaplains, and this is what I find:
Convicts Y-ll and Y-12. Case of two very young boys under sixteen of very good families. Were following the sea as a profession hitchhiking from their homes at the close of the lake navigation season to go to the home of relatives on the Atlantic coast, whence to ship aboard a deep sea ship. The two ran out of food and money when near their destination, and, finally, in a panic, took a car in which the keys had been left to complete the last lap of their trip. They were apprehended en route, taken before the local magistrate where, without counsel or opportunity to get help from their families, they frankly pleaded guilty and were promptly sentenced to three years in the penitentiary. It was their first offence. They did no damage to the car. Their destination was legitimate although the use of the car without permission was, of course, wrong. They come from solid law abiding families, were travelling at full permission of home and school authorities. They had unblemished records and were a couple of kids. Remote cause: nil. Immediate cause: hunger and panic. (These two convicts were since removed from the large penitentiary to which they had been sentenced to a smaller institution where more selected convicts are sent.)
It is difficult to believe a story like that, isn't- it? Here we have two boys under sixteen sent to the penitentiary under these conditions: and we must assume the facts to be true, since this is the report of the chaplain who interviewed these boys. I wonder who committed the greater wrong against society, the boys or the magistrate. During the Easter recess I was discussing this astounding case with a magistrate in my own province, who .suggested that the tendency in those prov-

Penitentiary Act
inces, presumably the maritimes, was to sentence convicts coming from other parts of Canada to the penitentiary so that their governments would not have to pay for the upkeep of the convicts. I cannot subscribe to that; I cannot believe it is true, but I am repeating what I have been told. Another suggestion was that the magistrates in those provinces are inclined to send convicts, especially young convicts, to the penitentiaries since there are no institutions in their own provinces where those boys might be sent, at least no fit and proper institution, and sending them to a penitentiary might be better than sending them to the provincial jails. Perhaps there is some truth in both statements that have been given me; and, if so, is it not high time we did something to bring about a unified system, especially a Borstal system for young offenders?
It is hard to believe that young boys under sixteen years of age would be sent to a penitentiary; yet if you read the report of the superintendent you will find tables of statistics on pages 73 and 74, which show that four boys under sixteen years of age form part of our penitentiary population. So I trust the minister will move soon, and move his commissioner to act soon, in the formation of a Borstal system, or at least in adopting the recommendations made by the commissioner, which I read a few minutes ago.
The bill before the house purports to bring about improvements in our penal system, and if it did this I would welcome it. To me, however, the core of the bill is a change from a three-man commission back to the old system of one boss for the whole organization, and I consider this an abandonment of the main recommendation of the Archambault report, which I consider one of the finest reports any royal commission ever made. Because that is the case I am very sorry, but I shall be forced to vote against second reading of the bill.

The question of reform is a very big one, I know; and I am coming back to the province of the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), where they have an excellent penitentiary at Westminster. I was going to say I had occasion to be there, and by that I mean I had occasion to visit it once. I learned a great deal from a man whom I now know very well, who spent sixteen years in that institution as a convict and is now out on ticket of leave. I think he has a broader knowledge of the workings of the convict mind than anyone I at least have ever met. His position on the human side of the story is this. We will say we go into an institution and grant a reform. One that he told me about, for example, was the right to talk in the cells after meals. If you know how these tiers of cells are arranged in our penitentiaries,
Penitentiary Act

they have solid walls between the individual cells and conversation is almost unheard of because immediately it becomes a babel of shouting from one place to another. As he told me, men who are anxious to work and who had drafting boards in their cells were trj'ing to learn something by way of enginee

ing-because they have a very good library i" that institution. But they were just stopped on account of the bedlam. This privilege wa'-granted by General Ormond, who was superintendent and a kindly disposed man; and the thing just came to nothing.
The answer to that was, he told me, that the young chaps were immediately convinced that the move was not made through the decency or kindness of the authorities, but that they were immediately persuaded by the old lags that this had been forced on them; and they assumed all the credit for the change which was made, as they assume credit for every change which is made. Therefore they become the heroes to these younger chaps who are in the institutions and are necessarily in association with these older men.
I am not going to advocate anything, but I am going to ask whether or not the government has given consideration to a law such as one finds in the state of New York, for example, where, after four convictions for a definite type of crime, a man is removed from circulation. It is the equivalent of life imprisonment, after four convictions. It seems to me there may be some good in that idea-perhaps not as strict as they have it; but I am suggesting that the government should consider it.

Maj* I say with respect to the three-man commission which my hon. friend has spoken about, and which he finds so objectionable, that I am unable to follow him there. Mr. Speaker, I shall not be long, because I spoke about this subject last year. However, in view of General Gibson's report, I wanted to make some further observations.
I feel that the general ought to be complimented on his report, because it indicates broad understanding and a progressive mind. I thought he rather caught the spirit of the Archambault report.
As I recall the report, it laid down three principles, namely segregation, classification and after-care. In his report, General Gibson covered the first two rather thoroughly. If I can make any suggestions it would be on minor points-perhaps minor is not the proper word to use. Perhaps I should say that I would address myself to a few matters which lack emphasis in the report.
With respect to the Borstal system, General Gibson says that the system offers the best known opportunity for the reformation and rehabilitation of those who have not yet become hardened criminals. With that we all agree. While the Borstal system is directed to the needs of wayward youths, we must bear

Penitentialy Act
in mind that almost everyone in penitentiaries at the present time was once of an age and character that the Borstal system might have been useful to him. This fact is obvious when one looks at the annual report of the superintendent of penitentiaries which, in table 5 on page 7 indicates that in seven penitentiaries in Canada 1,238 of a total inmate population of 3,362 are under the age of twenty-five years. Table 4 indicates that one-third of the offenders are serving terms of three years or less.
I thought for a few moments we might consider the need of employing Borstal tactics in our penal therapy. British statistics show that approxmately sixty per cent of discharged Borstal inmates do not appear before the courts for further convictions. We see that twenty per cent are reconvicted once, and the remainder once or more.
What is our record? Page 8 of the same report shows that in the fiscal year ended March 31. 1946, there were 708, or less than twenty per cent of offenders who had no previous convictions. Over one-half-to be exact, 1,802 of the total of 3,362 had from two to eight convictions. It is to be remembered that these figures do not take into account the large number of people found in the many reformatories, industrial schools and jails across the country. I think it is obvious that something must be done to correct such an alarming situation. There seems to be no reason why Canada should have a greater proportion of recurring criminal tendencies among those who are released from her institutions of correction. We do not have the crowded cities there are in England, a circumstance which is often a contributing factor. There are other reasons, but in the main it is that our penal therapy is out of date and inadequate and in some degree ineffective.
One of the chief contributing factors is the lack of education which is a great cause of delinquency. On page 75 of the report I came across these startling figures: Out of a total of 1,635 persons, fifty-eight could neither read nor write, eleven could only read and 1,293 had common school education.
General Gibson has not lost sight of that, and in section 18(b) on page 13 of his report he points out that a thorough survey of the methods in each penitentiary by an experienced educationalist is necessary. It is true the Archambault report made a similar recommendation. Like the speakers who have preceded me, my complaint is that the recommendations are not being implemented fast enough; that these are all fine intentions, but we are not moving along quickly enough.
There is another matter which is important and which I think should be brought to the attention of the house, the matter of prison discipline. This is a most important phase in reformatory treatment and it has been forcibly brought to our attention by a riot in Stony Mountain penitentiary. I should like to refer to an article in the Montreal Gazette setting out an interview with an ex-convict who had served some time there. There is no reason why he should not tell the truth and here is what he had to say:
The outbreak had been no massed riot and had been the result of petty punishments. A man smoking out of hours would be awarded seven days solitary confinement and a man snoring would get three or four days "for creating a disturbance."
And again:
It was the narrow petty penalizing which had been responsible for the outbreak. All the prisoners wanted was better conditions. They all realized they had to do their time, but they didn't see why their existence should be made intolerable.
General Gibson has not lost sight of that recommendation. There again we have the same difficulty. These matters are small, but they accumulate and cause mischief in the institution. I come now to something which I think has been overlooked in General Gibson's report, the matter of after-care. I consider this to be of paramount importance if we are to cure criminal tendencies in our young offenders. On page 67 of the report it is stated that of those discharged during the year, fifty-six were under the age of twenty-nine. Table 15 on page 13 shows that a total of 838 prisoners were interviewed by welfare organizations during the year, despite the fact that 1,061 were discharged during the same year. We may well ask ourselves: Where are those discharged people to go and what are they to do? Are they being ostracized by society? What means have we provided for the reestablishment of ex-prisoners as useful, contributive citizens in our society?

The Canadian penal association, under its new president, Major J. A. Then he goes on to say:
Your commissioner is of opinion that the activities of these societies should be encouraged and recognized and recommends that when a society demonstrates that it has been organized to carry out its duties with a reasonable degree of efficiency, provision should be made for it to receive financial assistance from the dominion government, based on the numbers released from federal institutions who have been assisted by its activities, to supplement the funds received from other sources.

debates is an awareness and recognition that the penal system of this country is inadequate and that there is urgent need for penal reform.
General Gibson holds that view and I am sure the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) holds that view. We must clearly understand, however, that General Gibson has grasped the principles involved and has attempted to meet the problem as he sees it. I should like to add a very few words to this debate, and I think I can sum up what I want to say by putting in a plea for more urgency. Let me say at once that I do not wish to underestimate the difficulties that exist, I know we cannot do everything overnight. Second, I believe that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) is just as humane a man as there is in this house and just as anxious to see this job done as anybody. Nevertheless I feel, as I look back over the last eight or nine years, and particularly over the last year, and particularly as I read this report of General Gibson, that there is no sense of urgency felt. There seems to me to be a fatal deliberation about the whole business, and the reason I deprecate that is the very reason given by my seatmate, the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith), that, while we are deliberating, day by day young men who perhaps were accidental criminals to begin with are being taken into the penitentiaries and becoming expert and perhaps permanent criminals by the very treatment we are giving them. That seems to be an undisputed fact. Therefore I suggest .hat there is an urgency, and if there is an urgency, frankly I do not find any sign of it in this report.
I would point out at this stage in my brief remarks that it has been stated in this house and never denied that we who rightfully regard

ourselves are so advanced, and are in many ways advanced, are nevertheless regarded as a backward nation in this respect. That statement has been responsibly made-and I repeat it and it has never, so far as I know, been denied in this house. If that is true I think that is the background which should cause us to feel a great sense of urgency, the evidence of which I have never been able to find.
The first reason why I feel this sense of urgency is lacking is put in my mind by reading paragraph 4 of the report, and if my inference is wrong I hope the minister will correct me. Mark you, here is a commissioner specially appointed, as I understand it, to get on with this special job and try to put into effect a report which came out nine years ago. I am not forgetting the war. Nevertheless the Archambault report is nine years old and there are reports behind that going back for thirty years. So that we are really in arrears thirty years. Paragraph 4 of General Gibson's report reads as follows:
During the past six months, as a result of the untimely death of Mr. P. M. Anderson, K.C., of the Department of Justice, your commissioner has been assigned to supervise directly the administration of the penitentiaries branch on behalf of the department and has thus been afforded an opportunity of observing and participating in the day to day management of the penitentiaries.
The commissioner puts that forward, that substantial work has been put upon him-if I am wrong in my inference I hope I shall be corrected-which I assume has slowed him up in the discharge of this special duty, which I am suggesting is so very important and urgent-
Then I come to paragraph 7 of this report, and here again I have a feeling that things are moving, yes, but there is no urgency; nobody is shoving the thing along as if it was an emergency to be dealt with, as I think it is. Paragraph 7 begins by saying this:
The reorganization of the penitentiary administration recommended by the royal commission has not yet .been undertaken.
I realize that you cannot suddenly undertake a reorganization. You have to give it thought. You cannot plunge into it in an ill-considered manner. But that sentence does not indicate that there has been any real sense of urgency, which is what I am asking for. The hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith), who speaks on this matter with more knowledge than I have, stated that segregation is urgent; it is so important and vital; he said that the difficulties in the way were not insuperable, and yet very little progress in that direction has been made.

Since I am not a lawyer it must seem strange for hon. members to hear me speak on this matter, but I have had more correspondence this session on this matter than on anything else. I am not going to dwell on the subject because it has been covered very well by all the speakers. I want to congratulate the . speakers from all parties who, in my opinion, approached this matter in a non-partisan way. I should particularly like to endorse the attitude taken by the hon. member for Spadina t(Mr. Croll) in his remarks to the minister.

While there may have been reasons for delay during war time, there are no reasons for delay now in putting the Gibson report into effect.
As I said a moment ago, I have had more correspondence on this matter than on anything else which affects my riding.

speechtext: You have more criminals.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext: That is unfair. My riding happens to be particularly interested in the youth of the country. Through you, Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the house on the attitude that it has taken on this matter in viewing it, not from a party point of view, but from the point of view of the welfare of the youth of the country.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
I regret that I was not in the house earlier this evening to hear the discussion that has taken place. I know I would have benefited had I had the privilege of hearing other hon. members who participated in this debate.
At this late hour I do not intend to speak at any length but, sir, over the years I have had some little experience with the results that flow from the operations of penitentiaries. I do not know what the opinion of previous speakers has been; but, in my opinion, while many changes must take place, while our system today is very antiquated, it has done a surprising work, having regard to the difficulties under which those who operate our penitentiaries are actually working. On occasion I have seen men who have served their terms come from the penitentiaries and return once more to a life of crime. In large measure society is responsible for that; for when they return to a life of crime, in many instances the cause is that, after their discharge from penal institutions, they have no opportunity to secure work and little opportunity to regain their place in society. We are all to blame for that. I think it only fair at the outset of my remarks to make that statement.
I realize the difficulties under which the penitentiaries are operating today. I know-some of the shortcomings in connection with the administration. In saying these things, however, I cannot do other than mention the fact that, while the Archambault report was handed down a good many years ago and while there may have been some explanation for not implementing many portions of that report during the war years, there were few excuses prior to the war and since the termination of hostilities there have been few excuses that the government could rely on.

Penitentiary Act
As I see the situation it is this. The officials of the penitentiaries operate under, as I said a moment ago, an antiquated system in respect of which there has been little change in the last 100 years. So far as the staffs are concerned, within their power they are trying to carry out their responsibilities, but as I hear their story they find themselves in a position of being subjected to too many regulations from headquarters in regard to the administration. There has been a dilatoriness about everything.
Mention has been made this evening-and I mentioned it myself-that the report was handed down some nine or ten years ago and little has been done. I think, sir, that if those who are inmates of the penitentiaries, and particularly those who are discharged from these institutions, were of such numbers as to make their influence felt, many changes would have taken place in the administration of penitentiaries as a result of the representations made by those who have been discharged. Look at it as fairly as we may, all of us realize that there are shortcomings, definite nonfeasance. Representations are made from time to time and reports are handed down, but how few of us are prepared to take the interest necessary to make a great issue of the matter of penitentiary reform in our country. In Britain they were prepared to do that, and great leaders took up the cudgels and led the way. In Canada it has been otherwise. Private institutions, charitable institutions have undertaken the work. The Canadian Prisoners' Association has done a remarkable work. At the convention recently held in the city of Windsor, recommendations were made that might well be brought before the house and possibly later in this debate an opportunity will be given for the purpose.
There are those who speak of the number of recidivists, and certainly the statistics show that there are great numbers. But that has not been my experience with those whom I have known who have served in penitentiaries. The proportion has not been great so far as Saskatchewan penitentiary is concerned. Certainly it has not been as high as in other penitentiaries across the country, and one of the reasons has been that we have not had there a meeting with the older prisoners. New prisoners who come in, many of them desiring to reform, later on come under the influence of older and more experienced men, but there we have not had so many of the old-timers, the dangerous criminals, and the result has been that many who have been discharged from that institution have returned to civil life and are making good citizens.
I think of one man whose case I brought to the notice of the house. I will not mention the name, but the facts regarding him
are in the knowledge of the former, and no doubt of the present, Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley). Some seventeen years ago a young man in Saskatchewan was sentenced to life imprisonment in the penitentiary. He served for a period of years. When he entered1 the penitentiary his idea was that he would endeavour to live down the crime he had committed. He was convicted of murder and there was a commutation. He served in the penitentiary for fifteen years. When he entered the penitentiary he was in grade two or three. He continued to take advantage of the opportunities there. He accepted positions of responsibility in the service and by 1941 or 1942 had passed examinations equivalent to entrance into university.
All through the years this man studied; all through the years he dreamed of his freedom when his crime should have been expiated, and in 1944 he was granted ticket of leave and was discharged from the penitentiary, subject to monthly report. He joined His Majesty's forces, became a non-commissioned officer with the rank of sergeant, served for a period of approximately two and a half years, was discharged with a perfect record and is today living in Saskatchewan, restored to the district in which his crime was committed, and there enjoying something of the appreciation of the people at large for what he has done and what he is now trying to do.
Sometimes we look at the dark side, but here is an example of a young man who has proven that if he is prepared to accept the responsibilities that rest upon him, if he is prepared to take advantage of what is offered today, small as it is, there is hope for our penal institutions. But just because of such an example-I have pointed out one and there are others-it does not mean that this is general. Later on as I speak, I intend to refer to other examples and then to place before the house a few suggestions.
One suggestion I make now. That young man today, after having served approximately thiee years in the armed forces, has returned to his own district and is still required to report to the mounted police every month. There is a change that could be effected. Remove that disability, because disability it is. The police know where he is. He wrote to me the other day and pointed out this situation, and he said, "I will do my part if only you are able to secure the support of those in charge of administration to relieve me from being penalized for the rest of my days and required to report".
There is my first suggestion, that when a man is discharged from the penitentiary he
Privilege-Mr. Chevrier

should be given an opportunity to become rehabilitated. Do not hang about his neck a mandatory order that requires him, wherever he is, to report each month his whereabouts and also that he is willing to return to penitentiary when he is called upon.
On motion of Mr. Diefenbaker the debate was adjourned.
